meta.blurb: Father Brown looks harmless. He is short and shabby, with a round face and a clumsy umbrella. But the master thief Flambeau cannot fool him, and one by one the strangest crimes in England start to make sense.
meta.bible: Father Brown: a small, round-faced Catholic priest from Essex, shabby and mild, with a large umbrella; he has heard so many confessions that he understands how evil thinks. Flambeau: a huge, clever French thief, later an honest private detective and Father Brown's friend. Aristide Valentin: head of the Paris police, a sceptical, logical Frenchman. Hampstead Heath: where the thief is caught. Harwich: the port where Valentin lands. Westminster: where the real cross is posted. The Blue Cross: a silver cross set with sapphires, carried from Essex. Vernon Hotel: a very grand small hotel in Belgravia, London, where the Twelve True Fishermen dine. Mr Lever: its owner. Mr Audley: the club's chairman. The Duke of Chester: its young vice-president. Colonel Pound: a stiff, silent member. Ruby Adams: a girl near Putney. Colonel Adams: her silent father. Sir Leopold Fischer: her rich godfather. John Crook: a young journalist and Socialist who loves Ruby. James Blount: a cheerful man from Canada who says he is an old friend of the Adams family and arrived a week too late to see Mrs Adams alive; he is really Flambeau in disguise. Florian: the famous French acrobat and actor whom Blount names as his friend; the policeman in the pantomime is a drugged stranger. The Flying Stars: three huge African diamonds. Boxing Day: the day after Christmas. John Turnbull Angus: a young Scottish artist. Laura Hope: a girl in a sweet shop in Camden Town. Isidore Smythe: a small, clever inventor of clockwork servants, now a millionaire. James Welkin: a tall man with a squint, who becomes a postman. Himylaya Mansions: the tall block of flats. Lucknow Mansions: where Flambeau lives. Ludbury: Laura's home town. Bohun Beacon: a hilltop village. Colonel Norman Bohun: a wild, wealthy colonel. Wilfred Bohun: his devout priest brother. Simeon Barnes: the huge blacksmith. Gibbs: the village cobbler. Mad Joe: a simple-minded village lad. Greenford: the nearby town. General Sir Arthur St Clare: a famous English general whose tomb is a national shrine. Olivier: the noble Brazilian leader. Captain Keith: St Clare's future son-in-law. Colonel Clancy: the Irish colonel. Major Murray: a stern officer from Ulster. Espado: a Brazilian spy called the Vulture. Black River: the battle. Belfast: where Murray is buried. Pantomime: the Christmas play in the hall; its parts are Harlequin (Blount), Clown (Crook), Columbine (Ruby), Pantaloon (the colonel) and the Policeman. Chloroform: the drug used on the policeman. Clockwork: Smythe's headless servants. Squint: Welkin's crossed eyes. Postman: Welkin's disguise, with his mail bag. Cobbler: Gibbs's trade. Smithy: the blacksmith's forge and yard. Liverpool Street: the London station. Victoria: the London district of the restaurant with striped blinds. Camden Town: where Angus meets Laura. Putney: where Ruby lives. Brazil: where the war was fought. Captain Keith: St Clare's future son-in-law, who wrote a book about him. The Sign of the Broken Sword: the inn at the end of the forest road. Congress: the great gathering of priests in London. Mrs Adams: Ruby's mother, who died a week before Blount came. Wilfred: the curate who dropped a small hammer from the church tower. Voice and tone: dry, witty and gently ironic; murders and deaths are stated plainly with no gore; Brown is humble and quiet, and every riddle has a simple answer.

The Paper Strip in the Window
The Dead Man in the Smithy Yard
Where a Wise Man Hides a Leaf
The Other Half of the Sword

beats.scene: A steamer comes alongside the pier at Harwich in the early morning light
beats.summary: In The Blue Cross, a steamer from the Continent touches the pier at Harwich and the passengers come ashore.

beats.scene: A neat man in plain holiday clothes walks down the gangway
beats.summary: Among the passengers is Aristide Valentin, head of the Paris police, dressed like any holiday traveller.

beats.scene: A hand rests on a loaded revolver and a police card inside a coat
beats.summary: Under his ordinary clothes Valentin carries a loaded revolver and a police card, for he has come to make the greatest arrest of the century.

beats.scene: Newspaper pictures show a giant thief laughing at the police of Europe
beats.summary: His prize is Flambeau, a huge and clever thief who has fooled the police of Europe for years and loves a joke as much as a jewel.

beats.scene: A poster in London announces a great gathering of priests from many countries
beats.summary: Flambeau has vanished from France and is thought to be in England, where a great gathering of priests is about to meet in London.

beats.scene: Valentin looks out of a train window, thinking hard, one finger raised
beats.summary: Valentin knows only one fact about Flambeau: he is enormously tall, and a man can change his clothes and face but not his height.

beats.scene: Valentin watches new passengers climb into a railway carriage at a country station
beats.summary: On the train to London Valentin studies every passenger at every station, looking for a tall man.

beats.scene: A tall farmer, a tall guard and a thin labourer stand on a platform
beats.summary: He rules out a tall farmer, a tall railway guard and a lean labourer, one after another, for each is exactly what he seems.

beats.scene: A short priest sits in a corner surrounded by brown paper parcels
beats.summary: The only traveller left to study is a short priest from Essex with a round face, brown paper parcels and a huge umbrella.

beats.scene: The priest bends to pick up his big umbrella from the floor
beats.summary: The priest fumbles with his umbrella and parcels like a helpless child, and Valentin dismisses him as perfectly harmless.

beats.scene: The priest holds a small brown parcel carefully on his knee
beats.summary: The priest says shyly that one parcel holds a silver cross set with blue stones, an old treasure of his church, which he is taking to London.

beats.scene: Valentin leans toward the priest with a warning finger raised
beats.summary: Valentin warns the priest that London is full of thieves, and the little man answers mildly that he has his own way of keeping it safe.

beats.scene: A crowded platform at Liverpool Street as the train empties
beats.summary: At Liverpool Street the carriages empty, the priest wanders into the crowd with his parcels, and Valentin loses sight of him.

beats.scene: Valentin stands alone on the station steps among cabs and newsboys
beats.summary: Alone in London with no clue at all, Valentin admits that his careful method has failed.

beats.scene: Valentin walks down a grey street, peering into shop windows
beats.summary: He decides to follow anything odd or out of place, for a thief in disguise must leave some mark of strangeness.

beats.scene: A small restaurant with striped blinds on a quiet street near Victoria
beats.summary: Tired and hungry, Valentin goes into a small restaurant with striped blinds in a quiet street near Victoria.

beats.scene: Valentin stirs his coffee and stares at the cup in disgust
beats.summary: He puts sugar in his coffee, but it is salt, and the salt-cellar is full of sugar.

beats.scene: A startled waiter stands beside the table as Valentin holds up the bowl
beats.summary: The waiter cannot explain the swap, and then remembers the two clergymen who sat at that very table.

beats.scene: A dark stain of soup runs down the wall opposite the door
beats.summary: A dark stain on the wall shows where one of the clergymen suddenly threw his soup, and then paid his bill as if nothing had happened.

beats.scene: The waiter points through the doorway up the road as Valentin hurries out
beats.summary: The clergymen left only a few minutes ago, and Valentin throws down some coins and runs out after them.

beats.scene: A greengrocer's stall where the labels on the nuts and oranges are swapped
beats.summary: At a greengrocer's stall Valentin sees that the labels on the nuts and the oranges have been swapped.

beats.scene: A red-faced greengrocer waves his arms and points up the road
beats.summary: The red-faced greengrocer says one clergyman knocked over his apples and the other paid for the damage.

beats.scene: A policeman on the corner points to a yellow bus climbing the hill
beats.summary: A policeman says two clergymen climbed onto a yellow bus bound for Hampstead.

beats.scene: Valentin and two policemen squeeze onto the top of a yellow bus
beats.summary: Valentin takes two policemen and climbs onto the top of the next yellow bus to Hampstead.

beats.scene: The bus climbs a long hill while Valentin watches every window
beats.summary: As the bus climbs north, Valentin watches every shop and window for the next sign of the strange.

beats.scene: A restaurant window with a star-shaped hole and glass on the pavement
beats.summary: Valentin sees a restaurant window with a star-shaped hole in the glass and stops the bus.

beats.scene: A cashier counts coins at a desk beside the broken window
beats.summary: The cashier says a clergyman struck the glass with his umbrella and paid the full price at once.

beats.scene: The yellow bus stops where the houses end and the open Heath begins
beats.summary: The bus carries them to the top of the hill, where the houses end and Hampstead Heath begins.

beats.scene: A woman behind a counter of sweets points toward the Heath
beats.summary: In a sweet shop a woman says a clergyman asked her to post a forgotten parcel to an address in Westminster.

beats.scene: Two black figures far away cross the green slope of the Heath at sunset
beats.summary: Valentin sees two dark figures far away on the Heath and hurries after them with the policemen.

beats.scene: Three men creep across open grass as the sun sinks red
beats.summary: The three detectives follow the two clergymen across the Heath as the sun sinks, keeping low to avoid being seen.

beats.scene: Two priests sit on an old bench in a hollow under dark trees
beats.summary: The clergymen sit down on an old bench in a hollow, one short and round, the other tall.

beats.scene: Three men lie flat in the bushes, listening hard
beats.summary: The detectives crawl through the bushes until they can hear the two clergymen talking quietly about reason and heaven.

beats.scene: The short priest talks calmly, gazing up at the first stars
beats.summary: The short priest says that reason is always reasonable, even in the farthest stars and beyond the edge of the world.

beats.scene: The tall priest shifts on the bench, hesitating
beats.summary: The tall priest answers that reason may fail in far worlds, where two and two might make five, and then he stops, as if he has said too much.

beats.scene: The tall priest stands up against the sunset, towering over the other
beats.summary: The tall priest stands, says that he is Flambeau, and holds out the parcel he took from the little priest.

beats.scene: Brown looks up at the giant, mild and unmoved, his hands on his umbrella
beats.summary: Brown, mild and unmoved, asks Flambeau if he is quite sure it is the right parcel.

beats.scene: Flambeau tears open a brown paper parcel and finds only paper and lead
beats.summary: Flambeau tears the parcel open and finds nothing but wrapping paper and a lump of lead.

beats.scene: Brown speaks gently as the giant stares down at him in disbelief
beats.summary: Brown explains that he swapped the parcels back, posted the real cross to Westminster, and left a trail of mischief for the police to follow.

beats.scene: Valentin steps out from behind the trees and the policemen close in
beats.summary: Brown says he knew Flambeau was no priest because he attacked reason; Valentin steps out, arrests him and bows to the little priest.

beats.scene: A small, grand hotel in Belgravia shines with lamps at evening
beats.summary: In The Queer Feet, the Vernon Hotel in Belgravia is small, grand and expensive, and its owner Mr Lever is proud of it.

beats.scene: Mr Lever in black inspects the hall while the waiters stand in a line
beats.summary: Mr Lever inspects his hall and his waiters before the guests arrive, for tonight's dinner is an important one.

beats.scene: Gentlemen in black evening dress arrive at the door one by one
beats.summary: The members of the club called the Twelve True Fishermen arrive for their yearly dinner in black evening dress.

beats.scene: The chairman, a young duke and a stiff colonel stand together in the hall
beats.summary: Mr Audley is chairman, the young Duke of Chester is vice-president, and Colonel Pound is a stiff and silent member.

beats.scene: A long table set for twelve with silver fish knives and forks
beats.summary: The long table in the private dining room is laid for twelve, with twelve silver fish knives and forks set with pearls.

beats.scene: Waiters in black and white move round the table among the guests
beats.summary: The waiters in black and white look much like the gentlemen they serve, for evening dress is almost the same for both.

beats.scene: Father Brown arrives at a side door with a big umbrella
beats.summary: Father Brown arrives at a side door of the hotel, called by a waiter who is very ill upstairs and has asked for a priest.

beats.scene: Brown sits by a bed in a small upstairs room, listening kindly
beats.summary: Upstairs Brown comforts the sick waiter and listens to him, and then goes down to write a note.

beats.scene: Mr Lever shows a shabby priest into a small room beside the cloakroom
beats.summary: Mr Lever, who does not want a shabby priest seen by his grand guests, shuts Brown in a small room between the glass office and the cloakroom.

beats.scene: Brown writes at a small table in a dim room, door ajar
beats.summary: Brown writes his note alone at the small table, with the door open a little to the passage.

beats.scene: Brown lifts his head, listening to footsteps in the passage
beats.summary: While he writes, Brown hears odd footsteps in the passage: a swift, light run, then a slow, heavy stamp, again and again.

beats.scene: Brown lays down his pen and counts the steps with a frown
beats.summary: The steps come again and again, and each time a board creaks in the same place.

beats.scene: Brown frowns in the dim room, imagining feet dancing along a corridor
beats.summary: Brown decides that the slow steps belong to an idle gentleman, but the swift, soft steps remind him of something he cannot place.

beats.scene: A tall elegant man in evening dress waits at the cloakroom counter
beats.summary: A tall, elegant man in evening dress comes to the cloakroom, asks for his hat and coat, and throws down half a sovereign; Brown says he must have silver in his pocket.

beats.scene: The tall man leaps over the counter but the small priest stands firm
beats.summary: The stranger vaults the counter and seizes the priest, who says that he is a priest and is ready to hear his confession.

beats.scene: The tall man sinks into a chair, pale and silent
beats.summary: The thief, struck by these words, collapses into a chair and stares at the little priest in silence.

beats.scene: Twelve gentlemen stare in shock at a table where the silver was
beats.summary: At the dinner the plates are cleared and the silver has gone, and Mr Lever says he never sent the waiter who took them.

beats.scene: Mr Audley rises at the head of the table with a hand raised
beats.summary: The chairman announces the loss, the waiters are questioned, and the company realises that a thief has played a waiter.

beats.scene: Father Brown lays shining silver forks on the cloakroom counter
beats.summary: Brown tells the thief that the slow steps and the swift steps were one man's, a gentleman's and a waiter's; the thief lays down the silver and bursts out through the window.

beats.scene: Gentlemen crowd round the cloakroom counter as a priest points at a burst window
beats.summary: Brown shows the astonished club the silver on the counter and the burst window, and the Twelve True Fishermen decide to wear green coats.

beats.scene: A frosty garden near Putney, where a girl scatters crumbs for the birds
beats.summary: In The Flying Stars, on Boxing Day near Putney, Ruby Adams feeds the birds in her father's garden.

beats.scene: A young man jumps down from the garden wall in front of a girl
beats.summary: The young journalist John Crook, who loves Ruby, jumps down from the garden wall in front of her.

beats.scene: Ruby and Crook talk on the frosty lawn, with the wall behind them
beats.summary: Crook talks about Socialism and the poor, and Ruby listens fondly and says that her silent father is expecting a guest.

beats.scene: A green car stops at the gate and an old man emerges
beats.summary: Ruby's rich godfather, Sir Leopold Fischer, arrives in a green car and emerges from his furs.

beats.scene: Three men wait on the steps to welcome an old man in furs
beats.summary: Colonel Adams, James Blount, a cheerful friend from Canada, and Father Brown welcome Sir Leopold at the door.

beats.scene: Sir Leopold holds up a flat case beside the hall fire
beats.summary: In the firelit hall Sir Leopold takes a flat case from his coat and says it is Ruby's Christmas gift.

beats.scene: Three huge diamonds blaze in an orange velvet case in a firelit hall
beats.summary: The case holds three huge African diamonds called the Flying Stars, because they have been stolen so often.

beats.scene: Sir Leopold holds one huge diamond up to the light and tells its story
beats.summary: Sir Leopold tells how thieves have chased the stones from owner to owner, and says he keeps them always about his person.

beats.scene: Crook scowls at the diamonds while Sir Leopold smiles in his chair
beats.summary: Crook says that such wealth in one small case is a scandal while so many are poor, and Sir Leopold begins to dislike him.

beats.scene: A messenger hands a letter to James Blount at the open front door
beats.summary: A messenger brings Blount a letter at the open front door, and he reads it with delight.

beats.scene: Blount waves a letter in the hall and tells everyone the news
beats.summary: Blount says the letter is from his old friend Florian, a famous French acrobat and actor, who is coming that night.

beats.scene: Blount stands in the middle of the hall, handing out parts with sweeping gestures
beats.summary: Blount proposes an old English pantomime for the evening, with himself as harlequin, Crook as clown, Ruby as columbine and the colonel as pantaloon.

beats.scene: Blount telephones in the hall while servants carry cardboard and paint
beats.summary: Blount telephones Florian and asks him to bring a policeman's costume, and the whole house begins to prepare.

beats.scene: The cast covers itself in silver paper, flour and paste jewels
beats.summary: The actors dress up in silver paper, flour and paste jewels, until nobody can tell who is who.

beats.scene: Father Brown wears a paper donkey's head while Blount holds a paper tail
beats.summary: Blount puts a paper donkey's head on Father Brown and pretends to pin a paper tail on Sir Leopold's coat.

beats.scene: The hall is a little theatre with a curtain, chairs and glowing lamps
beats.summary: That evening the hall is a theatre, with a curtain and rows of chairs, and neighbours and servants wait to watch.

beats.scene: A flour-white clown chases a pantaloon in a nightcap across the stage
beats.summary: The pantomime begins with Crook the clown and the pantaloon chasing each other across the stage, and the audience laughs.

beats.scene: A glittering harlequin dances over a limp policeman on a stage in a hall
beats.summary: The harlequin knocks down the policeman and tosses him about the stage like a sack, to the roars of the audience.

beats.scene: The curtain falls and Sir Leopold rises, feeling for something in his coat
beats.summary: When the curtain falls, the audience claps, and Sir Leopold stands up and begins to feel anxiously in his pockets.

beats.scene: Sir Leopold storms out of the hall, white-faced, as guests stare
beats.summary: Sir Leopold cries that the diamonds have vanished from his pocket and storms out of the hall.

beats.scene: A pantaloon in white paint faces an angry old man in a study
beats.summary: In the study Sir Leopold declares the diamonds stolen, and the colonel, still in his pantaloon paint, tries to calm him.

beats.scene: Sir Leopold points a trembling finger at Crook in his clown's flour
beats.summary: Sir Leopold accuses Crook, who turns out his pockets; Brown says a man who steals diamonds does not talk Socialism, and they should look for a stranger.

beats.scene: Guests search the hall and stairs among the torn paper scenery
beats.summary: The guests search the hall, the stairs and the scenery for the stones, but find nothing.

beats.scene: Father Brown bends over the motionless policeman on the curtained stage
beats.summary: The policeman is still lying on the stage where the harlequin left him, and Father Brown bends over him.

beats.scene: Brown speaks quietly to Colonel Adams while Blount stands stiff behind him
beats.summary: Brown asks the colonel when Mrs Adams died, and learns that Blount arrived from Canada a week too late to see her.

beats.scene: Brown sniffs the air near the policeman's pale face, frowning
beats.summary: Brown smells chloroform and finds that the policeman was drugged before the pantomime began.

beats.scene: Brown slips out of a garden door into the cold moonlight
beats.summary: Alone, Brown slips out through the garden door into the cold moonlight and walks toward the bare trees.

beats.scene: A glittering silver figure hangs in a moonlit tree above a small priest
beats.summary: In the moonlight Brown finds a glittering figure in silver paper crouched in a tree: it is Flambeau.

beats.scene: Brown looks up and speaks gently to the glittering figure in the branches
beats.summary: Brown praises Flambeau's plot and begs him to give back the stones and give up crime.

beats.scene: Diamonds fall sparkling into the frozen grass as a silver figure drops and flees
beats.summary: The diamonds fall from the tree, and Flambeau vanishes into the night: it is his last crime.

beats.scene: A Camden Town sweet shop with a window full of cakes
beats.summary: In The Invisible Man, John Turnbull Angus, a young Scottish artist, walks up a Camden Town street to a small sweet shop.

beats.scene: Angus at a small table orders a bun and a cup of coffee
beats.summary: Angus sits down in the shop and orders a bun and a cup of coffee from the girl who serves him, Laura Hope.

beats.scene: Angus leans toward a girl in an apron, who stands very still
beats.summary: Angus tells Laura that he loves her and asks her to marry him.

beats.scene: Laura sits down opposite Angus, her hands folded, sad but calm
beats.summary: Laura says she cannot answer until he has heard her story, and she sits down to tell it.

beats.scene: A quiet country town called Ludbury, with a market square and a church spire
beats.summary: Laura tells him that she comes from the small town of Ludbury, where two men once wanted to marry her.

beats.scene: A small, neat man works at a bench among cogs and little metal figures
beats.summary: The first was Isidore Smythe, a small, clever man who made clockwork servants and has since become a millionaire.

beats.scene: A tall man with a squint stands in a doorway, scowling
beats.summary: The second was James Welkin, a tall man with a terrible squint, whom Laura came to fear.

beats.scene: A girl at a cottage gate turns away from two men
beats.summary: Laura refused them both, because she loved neither, and she hoped they would forget her.

beats.scene: A long shadow of a tall man falls across an empty road
beats.summary: Welkin went away long ago, but lately Laura has had an uneasy feeling that he is somewhere near.

beats.scene: A small man in a top hat hurries into the sweet shop
beats.summary: As Laura finishes her story the door opens and a small man in a top hat hurries in: it is Isidore Smythe.

beats.scene: Smythe points to a strip of paper pasted on the shop window
beats.summary: Smythe points to a strip of paper on the shop window, which says that if Laura marries him he will die.

beats.scene: Smythe in his top hat holds out a bundle of crumpled letters
beats.summary: Smythe says he has already had five threatening letters at his flat, and nobody knows who brought them.

beats.scene: Angus and Smythe climb into a small car while Laura watches
beats.summary: Angus offers to help, and drives off with Smythe to his flat.

beats.scene: A tall block of flats stands at the top of a steep, snowy street
beats.summary: They drive up a steep hill to Himylaya Mansions, a tall block of flats where Smythe lives at the top.

beats.scene: Rows of headless clockwork servants stand along the walls of a flat
beats.summary: Smythe's flat is full of clockwork servants without heads, standing in rows like soldiers.

beats.scene: A scrap of paper in red ink lies among rows of headless clockwork servants
beats.summary: On the floor Angus finds a new note in red ink, threatening Smythe, which nobody can explain.

beats.scene: Angus talks quickly to Smythe, pointing to the door and the stairs
beats.summary: Angus decides that Smythe needs a detective, and promises to fetch his friend Flambeau.

beats.scene: Angus pays four men at the doors of the building, one by one
beats.summary: Before he leaves, Angus pays four men to watch the building: a porter, a doorman, a policeman and a chestnut seller.

beats.scene: A flat full of sabres, a Persian cat and a priest
beats.summary: Angus hurries to Lucknow Mansions, where Flambeau lives, and finds him with a small priest, Father Brown.

beats.scene: Three men sit by a window as the first snowflakes fall
beats.summary: Angus tells his tale, and as he talks the first flakes of snow drift past the window, as Brown said they would.

beats.scene: Three men in overcoats walk through falling snow toward a tall building
beats.summary: The three men set off through the falling snow to Himylaya Mansions.

beats.scene: Four watchers stand at their posts, shaking their heads firmly
beats.summary: The four watchers all swear that nobody has gone into the building.

beats.scene: Grey footprints cross the snowy doorway between the legs of a gold-braided doorman
beats.summary: Brown points to a line of footprints in the new snow, crossing the doorway beside the doorman, and nobody saw the man who made them.

beats.scene: Upstairs a dark stain on the floor of an empty flat among headless figures
beats.summary: Upstairs the flat is empty and a stain lies on the floor, but Smythe has gone.

beats.scene: A breathless policeman runs up the snowy road with news for Brown
beats.summary: Brown asks the policeman to search below the hill, and he runs back to say that Smythe's body has been found in the canal, killed by a stab.

beats.scene: Brown speaks quietly to a policeman, who stares at him in blank astonishment
beats.summary: Brown asks whether a light brown sack was found near the body, and nobody has found one.

beats.scene: Father Brown walks downhill in the snow, explaining, with two men beside him
beats.summary: Brown explains that people answer what you mean, not what you ask, so a man did go in and out unnoticed, for a postman is never noticed.

beats.scene: Father Brown puts a hand on a postman's shoulder in the snowy street
beats.summary: Brown stops a passing postman and lays a hand on his shoulder.

beats.scene: A postman turns on a snowy street with a terrible squint
beats.summary: The postman turns with a terrible squint: it is Welkin, who killed Smythe and carried his body away in his mail bag.

beats.scene: Two men walk away over white hills while a third runs back through snow
beats.summary: Angus runs back to Laura with the news, while Brown walks away over the hills with the murderer.

beats.scene: A steep village at dawn with a grey church tower above the roofs
beats.summary: In The Hammer of God, the village of Bohun Beacon, built on a steep hill, wakes at dawn beneath its church tower.

beats.scene: A huge blacksmith works at a glowing forge in a walled yard
beats.summary: The village blacksmith, Simeon Barnes, is a huge, grave man of great strength who goes to prayer meetings in the town of Greenford.

beats.scene: Two brothers meet in a village street at dawn, one in black
beats.summary: At dawn Colonel Norman Bohun, a wild and wealthy man, meets his devout brother Wilfred in the village street.

beats.scene: The colonel laughs carelessly while his pale brother pleads with him
beats.summary: Norman laughs and teases his brother, but Wilfred begs him to change his ways.

beats.scene: Wilfred points toward the smithy while the colonel shrugs
beats.summary: Wilfred warns Norman that the huge blacksmith has good reason to hate him.

beats.scene: The colonel strolls away whistling as the sun rises over the rooftops
beats.summary: Norman says he fears no blacksmith and strolls away whistling while the sun rises.

beats.scene: Wilfred goes into the dim church and kneels alone
beats.summary: Wilfred, the curate of the village church, goes inside to pray alone.

beats.scene: A cobbler works at his window while a simple lad wanders past
beats.summary: In the village street the cobbler Gibbs works at his window, and a simple-minded lad called Mad Joe wanders by.

beats.scene: The cobbler runs up the street toward the church, his apron flapping
beats.summary: Not long afterwards Gibbs runs to the church and tells Wilfred that the colonel lies dead in the smithy yard.

beats.scene: Wilfred runs down the steep street between cottages toward the forge
beats.summary: Wilfred runs down the steep street and finds a crowd at the gate of the smithy yard.

beats.scene: A man lies among hammers and iron in a smithy yard
beats.summary: The colonel lies dead among the hammers in the smithy yard, killed by a single terrible blow to the head.

beats.scene: The cobbler and the doctor stand beside the body, nodding grimly
beats.summary: The cobbler and the doctor say that only the huge blacksmith had the strength to strike such a blow.

beats.scene: Father Brown arrives at the yard gate with his umbrella, small and quiet
beats.summary: Father Brown, who has come to visit Wilfred, arrives at the yard and looks quietly at everything.

beats.scene: Brown crouches by the body and studies a small hammer
beats.summary: Brown picks up a small hammer and wonders why so big a man would use so small a hammer.

beats.scene: A police inspector speaks sharply to the blacksmith at the yard gate
beats.summary: The police inspector arrives, and Barnes the blacksmith, just back from Greenford, is arrested.

beats.scene: Two men from Greenford speak firmly to the inspector at the gate
beats.summary: Two friends from Greenford swear that the blacksmith spent the whole night at a prayer meeting, so he could not have done it.

beats.scene: A doctor whispers to a curate while a red-haired woman weeps on a bench
beats.summary: The doctor whispers that the blacksmith's wife may be guilty, and points to her weeping on a bench.

beats.scene: Brown shakes his head gently, speaking to the doctor
beats.summary: Brown tells the doctor that no woman could have struck such a blow.

beats.scene: Wilfred speaks eagerly, pointing toward the village
beats.summary: Wilfred suggests that Mad Joe might have done it, but Brown says that theory is not true.

beats.scene: The doctor stares at Brown, puzzled, as villagers whisper nearby
beats.summary: The doctor is puzzled and asks Brown whether he has a theory of his own.

beats.scene: The blacksmith faces the inspector in his yard and speaks of a thunderbolt
beats.summary: The blacksmith says no thing of flesh held that hammer, and that the blow was a thunderbolt from heaven.

beats.scene: Villagers whisper and cross themselves as clouds gather over the hill
beats.summary: The villagers murmur, and some are half inclined to believe the blacksmith's words.

beats.scene: Brown draws the doctor aside under a wall and speaks quietly
beats.summary: Brown draws the doctor aside and gives him two hints: it is a matter of physical science, and a flying hammer is nearest the truth.

beats.scene: The doctor frowns, gazing at the sky and the church tower above the roofs
beats.summary: The doctor puzzles over the hints but sees no answer, though his eyes wander up to the church tower.

beats.scene: Two priests walk side by side up the steep street toward the church
beats.summary: Brown asks Wilfred to show him the church, and the pale curate leads the way up the steep street.

beats.scene: Two priests climb a narrow stone staircase winding inside a tower
beats.summary: Inside the church Brown asks to go up the tower, and the two priests climb the winding stair.

beats.scene: Two priests stand on a high stone gallery above a small square yard
beats.summary: At the top they step out onto a high outer gallery, from which they can see the whole plain and the smithy yard far below.

beats.scene: Brown speaks quietly as Wilfred grips the stone rail, white-faced
beats.summary: Brown tells of a man who prayed in high places until he fancied himself God.

beats.scene: A small hammer falls through empty air from a great height
beats.summary: Brown says that even a small hammer dropped from such a height would strike like a bullet.

beats.scene: Wilfred puts one leg over the stone wall and Brown grabs his collar
beats.summary: Wilfred throws a leg over the wall, but Brown catches him by the collar and pulls him back.

beats.scene: Wilfred sits trembling on the stone floor, his face in his hands
beats.summary: Wilfred sits trembling on the stone floor, and Brown says that he knows what he did and will tell no one.

beats.scene: Brown speaks softly to Wilfred as the wind blows over the tower
beats.summary: Brown says that from the gallery Wilfred saw his brother in the yard below, and in a moment of anger let a hammer fall.

beats.scene: Wilfred weeps while Brown puts a gentle hand on his shoulder
beats.summary: Brown says that the anger Wilfred took for holiness was pride, the same pride that tempts a man to fancy himself God.

beats.scene: Brown stands and offers a hand to help Wilfred up from the floor
beats.summary: Brown says again that he will tell no one, and leaves the next step to Wilfred.

beats.scene: The two priests descend a winding stair, one behind the other
beats.summary: They go down the winding stair in silence and come out of the church into the sunlight.

beats.scene: Wilfred walks down the steep street toward the smithy yard
beats.summary: Wilfred walks down the steep street toward the smithy yard, with Brown a little behind him.

beats.scene: Wilfred speaks to the inspector at the gate of the smithy yard
beats.summary: At the gate Wilfred tells the inspector that he killed his brother.

beats.scene: The inspector stares in amazement as villagers gasp and the doctor stands still
beats.summary: The inspector is astonished, and the villagers gasp; the doctor remembers Brown's hints and understands.

beats.scene: The red-haired woman and the blacksmith stand together at the gate
beats.summary: The blacksmith is set free, and his wife runs to him and weeps with joy.

beats.scene: Father Brown walks away alone up the steep street with his umbrella
beats.summary: Brown walks away up the hill alone, and the church tower stands over the village in the sunlight.

beats.scene: Two men in black stand before a great metal tomb on a frozen night
beats.summary: In The Sign of the Broken Sword, Father Brown and Flambeau stand on a frozen night before the great metal tomb of General St Clare.

beats.scene: Wreaths and flowers lie piled at the foot of a gleaming tomb
beats.summary: St Clare was a national hero, and his tomb is a shrine where visitors lay wreaths and flowers.

beats.scene: Brown looks up at Flambeau, thoughtful, his hands on his umbrella
beats.summary: Brown asks Flambeau where a wise man hides a leaf, and Flambeau answers that it is in the forest.

beats.scene: Brown looks along a dark forest road in the moonlight
beats.summary: Brown asks what the wise man does if there is no forest, and says that he would grow one.

beats.scene: Two men walk away from a tomb along a frozen forest road
beats.summary: They leave the churchyard and walk along a frozen road through a dark forest toward an inn.

beats.scene: Brown speaks quietly as they walk, the moon behind the branches
beats.summary: Brown says that he will tell a story that every Englishman knows, the story of General St Clare.

beats.scene: A hot battlefield in Brazil with a river and tiny soldiers
beats.summary: St Clare fought a war in Brazil against the noble leader Olivier, and he attacked him at Black River with a small force.

beats.scene: A broken sword hangs round the neck of a hanged general in a tree
beats.summary: St Clare was beaten and captured, and he was later found hanged from a tree with his broken sword round his neck.

beats.scene: Flambeau waves a hand impatiently as they walk in the moonlight
beats.summary: Flambeau says it is a sad tale but not a mystery: a brave general was beaten and hanged.

beats.scene: Brown shakes his head gravely in the moonlight
beats.summary: Brown says there are two things nobody asks: why a clever general attacked with so small a force, and why the noble Olivier hanged his prisoner.

beats.scene: Brown reads a printed page in the moonlight on a forest road
beats.summary: Brown takes out a book by Captain Keith, St Clare's future son-in-law, and reads a page by moonlight.

beats.scene: Brown holds a book to the moon, one finger on a line
beats.summary: The first clue: Keith's book says that St Clare was no fool and that Olivier was no brute.

beats.scene: Brown traces a line on a printed page with his finger
beats.summary: The second clue: Olivier's own dispatch praises the English for their last stand.

beats.scene: Flambeau strides ahead through the dark woods, guessing aloud
beats.summary: Flambeau guesses that the general, afraid of madness in his family, wished to die in battle and took his own life in despair.

beats.scene: Brown shakes his head sadly as Flambeau turns to wait for his answer
beats.summary: Brown says that it is a clean story, but the truth is worse.

beats.scene: A dying Irish colonel cries out against a sword in a dim room
beats.summary: Brown tells of Colonel Clancy, an Irish officer who cursed the sword with his dying breath.

beats.scene: A stern officer stands apart from the rest in a camp
beats.summary: Brown tells of Major Murray, a stern officer from Ulster, who died in the war and was buried in Belfast.

beats.scene: A watchful man in a dark cloak leans over papers by candlelight
beats.summary: Brown tells of Espado, a Brazilian spy called the Vulture, whose papers were captured after the war.

beats.scene: A general on a white horse talks with a tall major
beats.summary: The soldier's diary among Espado's papers tells how the general spoke privately with Major Murray and then ordered the attack.

beats.scene: Brown stops on the forest road and looks up at the moon
beats.summary: Brown asks Flambeau what he makes of the clues, and Flambeau admits that he sees only scattered facts.

beats.scene: A small broken blade lies hidden in a grave under frost
beats.summary: Brown says that the other half of the broken sword lies in Major Murray's grave in Belfast.

beats.scene: A snapped sword and a fallen officer in a dim tent
beats.summary: Brown explains that the sword snapped in a man's body, so the tip was buried with him.

beats.scene: A wide field of fallen soldiers hides one body among many
beats.summary: Brown returns to his riddle: a wise man hides a leaf in the forest, and a dead body in a field of dead.

beats.scene: A battlefield at dusk under a darkening sky, covered with fallen soldiers
beats.summary: To hide the death of one man, the general led his army into a battle that could not be won.

beats.scene: A general counts silver coins in a candlelit tent at night
beats.summary: Brown says that St Clare, who seemed so noble, was a traitor who sold secrets to the spy Espado for money.

beats.scene: Two officers face each other in a dark tent, one holding a paper
beats.summary: Major Murray found out the treachery and faced the general, who killed him, and the sword snapped.

beats.scene: Soldiers march out in good order at dawn behind a white-haired general
beats.summary: At dawn the general ordered the attack with his small force, knowing it must fail.

beats.scene: English soldiers on a hot hill turn their faces toward their white-haired general
beats.summary: On the hill the English soldiers fight and fall, and the survivors begin to understand what the general has done.

beats.scene: A hanged general in a tree, a sword round his neck, and silent soldiers
beats.summary: The English officers, knowing the truth, hanged the general and hung his broken sword round his neck.

beats.scene: A few officers swear an oath in silence on a dark hill
beats.summary: The officers swore to keep the secret to save the honour of the army, and Clancy's dying curse was for the sword.

beats.scene: Flambeau stands silent on a frozen road, thinking, the forest around him
beats.summary: Flambeau is silent for a long time, shaken by the story.

beats.scene: Flambeau turns to Brown in the moonlight, asking a question
beats.summary: Flambeau asks whether anyone can prove the story, and Brown says that nobody can, for the proof is a broken blade in a grave.

beats.scene: A young woman at a lamplit window thinks of a soldier far away
beats.summary: Flambeau asks what to do with the secret, and Brown says that the general's daughter is to marry Captain Keith.

beats.scene: A frozen puddle shines under the moon on a forest road
beats.summary: Brown says that no innocent person will be blamed if they keep silent, for the general paid for his crime long ago.

beats.scene: Two men walk toward the pale edge of a forest, the trees thinning
beats.summary: Flambeau agrees to keep the secret, and the two friends reach the edge of the forest.

beats.scene: A lit window of an inn glows warm and yellow against the frost
beats.summary: A warm light shines ahead: it is the inn where they will spend the night.

beats.scene: An inn sign shows a broken sword swinging above a door
beats.summary: They reach the inn, whose sign shows a broken sword: the Sign of the Broken Sword.

beats.scene: Two men enter a warm inn with a big fire and a long table
beats.summary: They go inside, where a fire burns warmly, and call for hot drinks.

beats.scene: Brown warms his hands at the fire, small and quiet
beats.summary: Flambeau asks how Brown understands crime so well, and Brown says that he has heard so many confessions.

beats.scene: Two men sit by an inn fire under a sign of a broken sword
beats.summary: They sit by the fire in the warm inn, the secret is kept, and the story ends.

A1A2: In the story The Blue Cross, a boat reaches Harwich early in the morning.
The quiet man is Aristide Valentin, the head of the Paris police.
Under his coat he carries a gun and a police card.
He wants Flambeau, a clever thief who has tricked the police for years.
Flambeau is in England, and a great meeting of priests is coming.
Flambeau is very tall, and a man cannot hide his height.
On the train, Valentin looks carefully at every person who gets on.
He sees a tall farmer and a tall guard, but they are honest men.
Only a short priest is left, with brown paper parcels and a big umbrella.
The little priest drops his umbrella again, and Valentin thinks he is harmless.
The priest says he carries a silver cross with blue stones.
Valentin tells him to take care, because London has many thieves.
At Liverpool Street, the priest walks into the crowd and is gone.
Valentin stands alone in London with no idea where to go.
He will now look for anything odd or out of place.
Tired and hungry, he goes into a small restaurant with striped blinds.
He puts sugar in his coffee, but it tastes of salt.
The waiter looks at the bowl in surprise and cannot explain it.
A dark stain on the wall shows where a priest threw soup.
The two priests left a minute ago, so Valentin hurries after them.
At a fruit stall, the labels on the nuts and oranges are swapped.
A fruit seller says a priest knocked over his apples and went away.
A policeman says two priests took a yellow bus to Hampstead.
Valentin and two policemen climb on top of the next yellow bus.
The bus climbs north, and Valentin watches every shop and window.
In a restaurant window, there is a hole shaped like a star.
The cashier says a priest hit the glass and paid at once.
The bus stops at the top of the hill by the open Heath.
A woman says a priest asked her to post a parcel.
Far away on the Heath, two dark figures are walking together.
The three men follow the priests across the Heath at sunset.
The two priests sit on an old bench in a quiet hollow.
The three men lie in the bushes and listen to them talk.
The short priest says reason rules even among the distant stars.
The tall priest says that, far away, reason may not rule.
The tall priest stands and says that he is Flambeau.
The small priest looks up and quietly asks if he is sure.
Flambeau tears open the parcel and finds only paper and lead.
Brown says the cross is in the post, and he left a trail.
Valentin steps out, arrests Flambeau, and bows to the little priest.
In The Queer Feet, the Vernon Hotel in London is small but grand.
Mr Lever checks the hall and the waiters before the guests come.
Twelve gentlemen in black evening clothes arrive for a yearly dinner.
Mr Audley leads the club, and the young Duke of Chester is second.
The long table has twelve silver knives and forks set with pearls.
The waiters wear black and white, like the gentlemen they serve.
A small priest comes in by a side door with his umbrella.
Upstairs, Father Brown comforts the sick waiter and listens kindly.
Mr Lever puts the priest in a small room near the coats.
Brown sits alone in the small room and starts to write.
Father Brown hears strange footsteps in the passage outside the door.
The steps come again and again, always with the same small sound.
The slow steps belong to a gentleman, but the quick ones puzzle him.
A tall man in evening dress asks Brown for his coat.
The man jumps over the counter and grabs the little priest.
The man falls into a chair and looks very pale.
In the dining room, the silver forks and knives are gone.
The guests are shocked, and they see that a thief played a waiter.
The thief puts down the silver, jumps through the window, and is gone.
The club learns the truth and decides to wear green coats.
On Boxing Day near Putney, Ruby Adams feeds the birds in the garden.
A young man jumps down from the wall, and it is John Crook.
Crook talks about the poor, and Ruby listens with a smile.
A green car arrives, and an old man climbs out of his furs.
Three men welcome Sir Leopold at the door, one of them Father Brown.
Sir Leopold takes out a small case and says it is a gift.
In the case are three huge diamonds called the Flying Stars.
Many thieves have tried to steal the diamonds, but Sir Leopold laughs.
Crook says that such rich gifts are wrong, and Sir Leopold looks angry.
A messenger brings a letter to James Blount at the door.
The letter says a famous French actor will visit that night.
Blount plans a Christmas play and gives everyone a part.
Blount telephones his friend and asks for a policeman's costume.
They cover themselves in silver paper and white flour.
Blount puts a paper donkey's head on Father Brown, laughing.
That night the hall is a theatre, and everyone waits to watch.
The play begins, and the clown and pantaloon make everyone laugh.
The harlequin knocks the policeman down and throws him about.
The curtain falls, and Sir Leopold searches his coat pockets.
Sir Leopold cries that the diamonds have gone and storms out.
In the study, Sir Leopold says the diamonds were stolen from him.
Sir Leopold points at Crook and says he is the thief.
They search the hall and the stairs, but find nothing.
The policeman is still lying on the stage, and Brown looks closely.
Brown asks when Mrs Adams died, and the answer surprises him.
Brown finds out that the policeman is sleeping because of a drug.
Brown goes quietly out of the garden door into the moonlight.
Brown finds a man in silver paper sitting in a tree.
Brown asks Flambeau to give back the diamonds and stop stealing.
The diamonds fall from the tree, and Flambeau runs away.
In The Invisible Man, a young artist goes to a sweet shop.
He orders a bun and coffee from a girl named Laura Hope.
Angus asks Laura to marry him, and she stands very still.
Laura says he must hear her story before she can answer.
In Ludbury, her home town, two men wanted to marry her.
Isidore Smythe was a small man who made clockwork servants.
The other was James Welkin, a tall man with a bad squint.
Laura said no to both men, because she loved neither.
Welkin went away long ago, but Laura feels he is near.
Just then a small man in a top hat comes into the shop.
Smythe points to a strip of paper stuck on the window.
Smythe says he has had five threatening letters at his flat.
Angus offers to help, and goes with Smythe to his flat.
They drive to Himylaya Mansions, a tall block of flats.
His flat is full of clockwork servants with no heads.
Angus finds a new note in red ink on the floor.
Angus says he will fetch a friend, the detective Flambeau.
Angus asks four men to watch the door of the building.
Angus finds Flambeau at home with a small priest.
As Angus tells his story, the first snow starts to fall.
The three men walk through the snow to Himylaya Mansions.
All four men swear that nobody has gone into the building.
Brown shows them footprints in the snow beside the door.
In the flat, there is a stain on the floor and no Smythe.
The policeman runs back and says they found Smythe's body.
Brown asks about a light brown sack, but nobody has found one.
Brown says people answer what you mean, not what you ask.
Brown stops a postman in the street and touches his shoulder.
The postman has a bad squint, and it is Welkin.
Angus goes back to Laura, and Brown walks away with Welkin.

Two brothers meet in the street at dawn: Norman and Wilfred.
Wilfred begs his brother to stop living such a wild life.
Wilfred warns his brother that the blacksmith hates him.
Norman laughs, and walks away whistling toward the forge.
Wilfred goes into the church to pray alone.
Gibbs the cobbler works in the village, and Mad Joe wanders past.
Gibbs runs to the church and tells Wilfred his brother is dead.
Wilfred runs down the steep street to the smithy yard.
The colonel lies dead among the hammers in the smithy yard.
The doctor says only the blacksmith is strong enough to do this.
Father Brown, a friend of Wilfred, arrives and looks around.
Brown looks at a small hammer and wonders about it.
The police arrive, and they arrest Barnes the blacksmith.
Two friends say Barnes was at a prayer meeting all night.
The doctor whispers that the smith's wife may have done it.
Brown says that no woman could strike such a blow.
Wilfred says Mad Joe might have done it, but Brown disagrees.
The doctor asks Brown if he has any idea of his own.
Barnes says that no man struck the blow, only God.
The villagers whisper, and some of them believe the blacksmith.
Brown takes the doctor aside and gives him two hints.
The doctor thinks hard about the hints but finds no answer.
Brown asks Wilfred to show him the church.
The two priests climb a narrow stair inside the church tower.
They stand on a high gallery above the village and the fields.
Brown speaks of a man who prayed in high places.
A small hammer dropped from here would fall like a bullet.
Wilfred climbs onto the wall, but Brown pulls him back.
Wilfred sits trembling, and Brown says he knows the truth.
Brown says Wilfred dropped the hammer from the tower in anger.
Wilfred cries, and Brown puts a hand on his shoulder.
Brown says he will tell no one, and the next step is Wilfred's.
The two priests go down the long stair without a word.
Wilfred walks down the steep street toward the smithy yard.
At the gate, Wilfred tells the inspector that he killed his brother.
The inspector is shocked, and the villagers gasp aloud.
The blacksmith is free, and his wife runs to him.
Brown walks away alone, and the tower stands over the village.
On a frozen night, Brown and Flambeau stand before a great tomb.
St Clare is a great hero, and people bring flowers to his tomb.
Brown asks where a wise man hides a leaf.
Brown asks what the wise man does if there is no forest.
They leave the tomb and walk along a frozen forest road.

Brown says that two things in the story do not fit.
Brown takes out a book and reads a page in the moonlight.

Flambeau guesses the general wanted to die in battle.
Brown says it is a clean story, but the truth is worse.
Brown tells of Colonel Clancy, who cursed a sword while dying.
Major Murray was a stern officer from Ulster.
Brown tells of Espado, a spy called the Vulture.
The diary says the general spoke with Murray, then ordered the attack.
Flambeau says he cannot see a pattern in these clues.
Brown says half the sword lies in a grave in Belfast.
The sword broke inside a man, and was buried with him.
A wise man hides a body among many dead bodies.
To hide one death, the general made a whole battlefield.
Brown says the general sold secrets for money.
Murray found out the secret, and the general killed him.

The soldiers fight bravely, and many of them fall on the hill.
His own officers hanged him, and hung the broken sword on him.
The officers kept the secret to save the honour of England.
Flambeau says nothing for a long time on the road.

Flambeau asks what to do with the secret.

B1B2: The Blue Cross begins on a bright morning at Harwich, where a steamer from the Continent has just touched the pier. Passengers pour down the gangway in a noisy crowd, and no one pays much attention to a quiet man in plain clothes.
The quiet man is Aristide Valentin, head of the Paris police and the most famous detective in Europe. He is dressed like any other holiday traveller, and no one on the pier guesses who he is.
Under his plain coat Valentin carries a loaded revolver and a police card. He has crossed the sea to make the greatest arrest of the century.
His prize is Flambeau, a huge and clever thief who has made fools of the police of Europe for years. Flambeau loves a joke as much as he loves a jewel, and every café in Paris has a story about him.
Flambeau has vanished from France, and Valentin is certain that he has crossed to England. Priests from many countries will soon meet in London, and a crowd is always a good place for a thief.
Valentin knows only one sure fact about Flambeau, which is that the thief is enormously tall. A man can change his clothes and his face, but he cannot easily change his height.
On the train to London Valentin studies every passenger at every station. He watches each new face as it enters, and he looks most carefully at the tall ones.
One by one he rules out a tall farmer, a tall railway guard and a long, thin labourer. Each of them is plainly what he seems to be, and none of them has the quick, clever eyes of a master thief.
The only traveller left is a short priest from Essex, sitting in the corner with a round, dull face. He has several brown paper parcels around him and a huge umbrella that keeps sliding to the floor.

The priest drops his umbrella yet again and gathers up his parcels with a worried little frown. Valentin watches him for a moment, decides that he is as harmless as a child, and turns back to the window.

The priest explains, with a shy smile, that one of his parcels holds a silver cross set with blue stones. It is a very old treasure of his church, and he is taking it to the great gathering of priests in London.
Valentin, half smiling, warns the priest that London is full of thieves and that he should guard such a treasure. The little man answers mildly that he has his own way of looking after it.
The train runs into Liverpool Street and the carriages empty in a rush of voices and luggage. The little priest wanders off into the crowd with his parcels, and Valentin loses sight of him at once.
Alone on the steps of the station, Valentin faces the truth that he has no clue at all. His careful method has failed, and the thief he is hunting could be anywhere in the huge city.
Then Valentin decides to use a different method, one that does not depend on height. A clever thief in disguise will always do something odd, so Valentin will follow whatever is out of place.
He walks a long way through grey, quiet streets until he is both tired and hungry. Near Victoria he sees a small restaurant with striped blinds and goes in to rest.
He orders coffee and stirs in a spoonful of sugar from the bowl on the table. One sip tells him it is salt, and when he looks again he finds that the salt-cellar is full of sugar.
Valentin calls the waiter, who looks at the bowl in honest surprise. The man swears that both pots were right this morning, and then he slowly remembers the two clergymen who sat at this very table.
The waiter points to a dark stain on the wall opposite the door. One of the two clergymen, he says, suddenly threw his soup across the room and then paid his bill as if nothing had happened.
The two clergymen left only a few minutes ago, the waiter says, and went up the road toward the shops. Valentin throws some coins on the table and runs out into the street.
A few streets away Valentin comes to a greengrocer's stall piled high with fruit and nuts. The label on the nuts says oranges, and the label on the oranges says nuts.

The red-faced greengrocer is waving his arms, and he tells Valentin that one clergyman has just knocked over a heap of his apples. The other clergyman paid for the damage, he says, and then both of them walked off up the road.
At the corner a policeman tells Valentin that two clergymen climbed onto a yellow bus a few minutes ago. The bus was going to Hampstead, he says, and it is probably still climbing the hill.
The next yellow bus for Hampstead rattles up to the stop, and Valentin climbs onto the top deck with the two policemen. The seats are hard and the wind is cold, but he does not care.
The bus climbs slowly north, past rows of shops and long, dull streets of houses. Valentin watches every window and doorway, and the policemen beside him begin to wonder what he is looking for.
Suddenly Valentin springs up and stops the bus, for he has seen a restaurant window with a star-shaped hole in the glass. It is the first thing that really looks like a clue, and he runs inside.
Inside, the cashier is busy with coins at a desk beside the broken window. A clergyman struck the glass with his umbrella, the cashier says, paid the full price at once, and walked on without a word.
The bus carries them on to the top of the hill, where the houses end and the wide Heath begins. Valentin jumps down and looks across the grass, but the two clergymen are nowhere in sight.
In the sweet shop a woman remembers two clergymen very well. One of them, she says, asked her to post a forgotten parcel to an address in Westminster, and she has already sent it off.
Valentin looks where she points and sees two dark figures far away across the grass, one tall and one short. He calls the policemen and sets off after them at a fast walk.
The Heath is wide and empty, and the sun is sinking behind the trees in streaks of red and gold. Valentin and the policemen follow the two clergymen at a distance, keeping low among the bushes.
At last the two clergymen reach a hollow with an old wooden bench and sit down together. One is short and round, the other is tall, and both are black shapes against the sky.
Valentin and the policemen crawl through the bushes until they are close enough to hear. To their surprise the clergymen are talking in low, calm voices about reason, and about heaven.
The short priest looks up at the first stars and says that reason is always reasonable. He believes that it rules even in the farthest heaven, where nothing can be true that is against it.
The tall priest answers that nobody can be sure about worlds so far away. Perhaps there, he says, reason is not the rule at all, and he stops, as though he has said too much.
The tall priest rises to his full height, and he is huge against the red sky. He says that he is Flambeau, and he holds out the parcel that he has taken from the little priest.
The little priest does not jump or cry out, and his round face stays perfectly calm. He only looks up at the giant and asks mildly whether Flambeau is quite sure that he has taken the right parcel.
Flambeau tears the string and the paper apart with his huge hands. Inside there is no cross at all, only a lump of lead and some folded sheets of paper.
Brown explains that he saw Flambeau swap the parcels and quietly swapped them back again. The cross is safe in the post, he adds, and the salt, apples and window were a trail for the police.
Brown says he knew the man was no priest, because he attacked reason, and that is bad theology. Then Valentin and the policemen step out of the trees, arrest the thief, and bow to the little priest.
The next story, The Queer Feet, begins at the Vernon Hotel, a small and very grand place in Belgravia. Only rich and famous guests come here, and its owner, Mr Lever, guards its good name carefully.
Mr Lever walks through the hall and the dining room with a critical eye. The waiters stand in a neat line in their black coats and white shirts while he checks every detail.
The guests are the members of a club called the Twelve True Fishermen, who meet at the hotel for a dinner every year. They arrive one by one in black evening dress, and they look very serious.
The chairman is Mr Audley, a dignified man, and the vice-president is the young Duke of Chester. Beside them stands Colonel Pound, a stiff and silent member who seems to disapprove of everything.
In the private dining room the long table is laid for twelve, and the silver gleams under the lamps. The pride of the club is its twelve fish knives and forks, each one set with pearls.
The waiters move quietly around the table in black coats and white shirts. In the evening, the dress of a waiter is almost the same as the dress of a gentleman.

While the dinner is being prepared, a short priest in a shabby coat arrives at a side door with his umbrella. It is Father Brown, who has been sent for by a waiter who is ill upstairs and has asked to see a priest.
Upstairs Father Brown sits beside the sick waiter and listens to him with great kindness. When the man has finished speaking, the priest comes down the stairs to write a note.
Mr Lever does not want a shabby priest to be seen by his grand guests. He shows Brown into a small room between the glass office and the cloakroom and asks him to write there.
The room is small and rather dim, with a narrow window and a table in the corner. Brown sits down alone with his pen, and through the open door he can hear the sounds of the hotel.
While Brown writes, he hears footsteps in the passage, and they are very odd. First comes a swift, light run, and then a slow, heavy stamp, and then the swift run again.
The steps come again and again, and each time they pass there is the same faint creak. Brown puts down his pen and listens with his head on one side, trying to understand what he hears.

Brown decides that the slow, heavy steps belong to an idle gentleman with nothing to do. The swift, soft steps are those of a man who is busy, and they remind him of something he cannot quite remember.

A tall, elegant man in evening dress comes to the cloakroom counter and asks for his hat and coat. He throws down half a sovereign, but Brown looks at him and says quietly that he must have silver in his pocket.
The man leaps over the counter and seizes the little priest by the collar. Brown is not afraid, and he says that he is a priest and is quite ready to hear the man's confession.
The thief lets go of the priest, sinks into a chair, and stares at him in silence. His face has turned white, and he looks like someone who has seen something he cannot understand.
Meanwhile, in the dining room upstairs, a terrible discovery is made. The plates have been cleared away by a waiter, and the twelve silver fish knives and forks have gone with them.
Mr Audley rises at the head of the table and announces the loss in a trembling voice. The waiters are questioned, and at last everyone understands that a thief has played the part of a waiter.
Brown tells him that the slow steps and the swift steps were one man's, a gentleman's and a waiter's. Then the thief lays the silver on the counter and bursts out through the window.

The members crowd into the cloakroom and find the silver on the counter beside the burst window. Brown explains that one man played both the gentleman and the waiter, so the club decides to wear green coats.
The Flying Stars begins on Boxing Day, the day after Christmas, in a frosty garden near Putney. A girl called Ruby Adams is scattering crumbs for the birds, and her cheeks are red with the cold.
Suddenly a young man jumps down from the garden wall and lands in front of her. He is John Crook, a journalist, and he is very much in love with Ruby.
Crook is a Socialist, and he cannot stop talking about the poor and the rich. Ruby listens with a smile, although she tells him that her father, Colonel Adams, is expecting an important guest.
A green car stops at the gate with a great noise, and servants hurry to help the passenger. Out of a heap of furs comes Sir Leopold Fischer, Ruby's rich godfather, who is old and rather stiff.
On the steps of the house three men wait to welcome the guest. They are Colonel Adams, a cheerful man called James Blount, and a small priest in a shabby coat, Father Brown.
In the firelit hall Sir Leopold takes a flat case from his coat with a grand gesture. He tells Ruby that this is her Christmas present, and he asks everyone to come close.
Inside the case, on a bed of orange velvet, lie three huge diamonds that blaze in the firelight. They are African stones called the Flying Stars, because they have been stolen so many times.
Sir Leopold tells the company how thieves have chased the stones from one owner to another. He says with a laugh that he is not afraid of any thief, because he keeps them always about his person.
Crook cannot keep quiet, and he says that such wealth in a single case is a scandal when so many are poor. Sir Leopold frowns, and from that moment he dislikes the young man.
Just then a messenger arrives at the open front door with a letter for Mr Blount. He reads it quickly, and his cheerful face lights up with delight.
Blount tells the company that the letter is from his old friend Florian, a famous French acrobat and actor. Florian is coming to the house that very night, and Blount is as excited as a schoolboy.
Blount cries that they must put on an old English pantomime that very night. He will be the harlequin, Crook the clown, Ruby the columbine, and the colonel the pantaloon.
He telephones Florian and asks him to bring a policeman's costume for the pantomime. At once the whole house is full of running servants, cardboard, paint and old curtains.
The cast dresses in silver paper and white flour, and sticks bright paste jewels on their costumes. Soon the hall is full of glittering strangers, and it is hard to tell who is who.
Blount, in high spirits, puts a paper donkey's head on Father Brown, who bears it with a smile. Then he pretends to pin a paper tail on the back of Sir Leopold's coat.
By evening the hall has been turned into a little theatre with a curtain and rows of chairs. Servants and neighbours fill the seats, and Sir Leopold sits in the front row in his furs.
The pantomime begins with a clown and a pantaloon chasing each other across the little stage. The audience laughs and claps, and even Sir Leopold allows himself a thin smile.
Then the glittering harlequin knocks the policeman to the floor and tosses him about like a sack. The audience roars with laughter, for the policeman seems to have no bones at all.
When the curtain falls, the whole hall claps and cheers. But Sir Leopold has risen to his feet, and he is feeling anxiously in all his pockets.
Sir Leopold cries out that the diamonds have vanished from his pocket. He storms out of the hall with a face as white as his hair, and the cheerful noise stops at once.
In the study Sir Leopold declares that the stones have been stolen while he sat watching the play. The colonel, still in his pantaloon paint, tries to calm him, but it is no use.

Sir Leopold points a shaking finger at Crook, the Socialist, and says he must be the thief. Crook turns out his pockets, and Father Brown says gently that a man who steals diamonds does not talk Socialism.
Everyone searches the hall, the stairs, the cloakroom and even the paper scenery on the stage. They find paste jewels and torn ribbons, but there is no sign of the diamonds.
In all the confusion nobody has noticed that the policeman is still lying on the stage where he fell. Father Brown bends over him and finds that he has not moved at all.
Brown asks the colonel quietly when his wife died, and learns that she died a week before Blount arrived from Canada. Blount had come to see an old friend, it seems, but he had come too late.
Brown notices a sweet, strange smell near the policeman's face and recognises chloroform. The man was not acting at all, for he was drugged before the pantomime began.
While the others are still arguing, Brown slips out through the garden door into the cold moonlight. He walks across the frozen lawn toward the bare trees, as quietly as a cat.
High in a bare tree something glitters in the moonlight. It is a man in silver paper, and Brown calls up to him, for he knows that the man is Flambeau.
Brown speaks gently to Flambeau, praising the cleverness of the plot, which used a false friend, a pantomime and a drugged man. Then he asks him to give back the stones and to give up crime for ever.
There is a long silence, and then something sparkles as it falls from the tree into the grass. Flambeau disappears into the night, and this is the last crime that he ever commits.
The Invisible Man begins in Camden Town, in a street of small shops. A young Scottish artist called John Turnbull Angus walks up to a sweet shop with a window full of cakes.
He sits at a small table and orders a bun and a cup of coffee. The girl who serves him is Laura Hope, and he has come here mainly to see her.
Angus lays down his spoon and says plainly that he loves Laura and wants her to marry him. She stands very still, and for a moment she does not seem to breathe.
Laura answers that she likes him very much, but that she cannot reply until he knows her story. She sits down opposite him and folds her hands, and Angus waits.
Laura explains that she comes from a small town called Ludbury, where she grew up. Two men there wanted to marry her, and she has never forgotten either of them.
The first was Isidore Smythe, a small, neat man with a clever pair of hands. He invented clockwork servants that could do the work of real servants, and he has since become a millionaire.
The other was James Welkin, a tall man with a terrible squint, whose ways frightened her. She did not like him, and as time went by she became afraid of him.
Laura refused them both, because she loved neither of them. She hoped that they would forget her, but she was not sure that they would.
Welkin went away long ago, and no one in Ludbury knew where he had gone. But lately Laura has had an uneasy feeling that he is somewhere near, watching.
Just as Laura finishes her story, the shop door opens with a bang. A small man in a top hat hurries in, and she gasps, for it is Isidore Smythe himself.
Smythe points to a strip of paper pasted on the shop window, in thin, neat handwriting. It says that if Laura marries him, he will die.
Smythe says that this is not the first warning, for five threatening letters have come to his flat. Nobody ever sees who brings them, and he is very frightened.
Angus, who is brave and a little jealous, says that he will go with Smythe to look at the letters. Laura begs them to be careful as the two men climb into the small car.
The little car climbs a steep road to Himylaya Mansions, a tall new block of flats. At the entrance stands a doorman in a coat covered with gold braid.
Smythe's flat is full of clockwork servants that stand in rows like soldiers, and none of them has a head yet. He builds them here, and the sight is rather strange.
On the floor among the figures Angus finds a new note written in red ink. It threatens Smythe again, and no one can say how it came into the flat.
Angus decides that Smythe needs a detective, and he knows exactly the man. His friend Flambeau gave up crime long ago and now works as a private detective.
Before he leaves, Angus asks four men to watch the building: a porter, a doorman, a policeman and a man selling chestnuts. He pays each of them well and tells them to watch for anyone who goes in.
Angus hurries to Lucknow Mansions, where Flambeau lives among sabres and a Persian cat. He finds him sitting with a small priest, Father Brown.
Angus tells his story from the beginning, while Flambeau listens with interest. As he talks, the first flakes of snow drift past the window, just as the little priest had said they would.
Flambeau and Brown agree to help, and the three men walk through the thickening snow to Himylaya Mansions. The street is white and quiet, and their feet make almost no sound.
At the building the four watchers stand at their posts, white with snow. Each of them swears that nobody has gone in or out since Angus left.
Brown points to a line of grey footprints in the new snow. They cross the doorway right beside the doorman, who has not noticed them at all.
They hurry upstairs to the flat, but Smythe is not there. The headless figures stand in their rows, and on the floor there is a dark stain that nobody can explain.

Brown quietly asks the policeman to search the streets and the canal below the hill. A few minutes later the man comes running back, breathless, to say that Smythe's body is in the canal, killed by a stab.
Brown asks the policeman whether anyone has found a light brown sack near the body. The man is astonished, and says that nobody has, and Brown nods as if that is what he expected.
Walking downhill, Brown explains that people answer what you mean, not what you ask. The watchers said that nobody had gone in, but they meant nobody unusual, and a postman is never noticed.
At the bottom of the hill a postman is walking through the snow with a heavy bag on his back. Brown steps up to him, lays a hand on his shoulder, and says a few quiet words.
The postman turns round, and he has a terrible squint. He is James Welkin, who killed Smythe in his flat and carried the body away in his mail bag.
Angus hurries back to Laura with the news that she is safe at last. Brown walks away over the snowy hills with the murderer, and he listens to him for a long time.
The Hammer of God is set in Bohun Beacon, a village built on a very steep hill. At dawn the church tower rises above its roofs, and the streets are still empty.
The village blacksmith is Simeon Barnes, a huge, grave man of enormous strength. He is deeply religious, and he walks to the nearby town of Greenford to take part in prayer meetings.
In the grey light two brothers meet in the street. Colonel Norman Bohun is a wild, wealthy man, and his brother Wilfred is a quiet, devout priest.
Norman laughs and teases Wilfred about his long face and his prayers. But Wilfred, who has been awake all night, begs him in a low voice to change his ways.
Then Wilfred warns his brother about the huge blacksmith, Simeon Barnes. The smith has good reason to hate the colonel, he says, and a man of that strength can be dangerous.
Norman says that he is not afraid of any blacksmith, and he strolls off whistling as the sun rises over the roofs. Wilfred watches his brother go, and his lips move as if in prayer.
Wilfred, who is the curate of the village church, turns in at the porch and goes inside to pray alone. The church is cold and dim, and the only sound is the wind in the tower.
In the village street Gibbs, the cobbler, is working at his window. A simple-minded lad called Mad Joe wanders slowly by, talking to himself, as he often does.
Not long afterwards the cobbler comes running up the street to the church, out of breath. He tells Wilfred that the colonel lies dead in the smithy yard.
Wilfred runs down the steep street so fast that he almost falls. At the gate of the smithy yard a crowd has gathered, and it parts without a word to let him through.
The colonel lies on his back among the hammers and scraps of iron. He has been killed by a single terrible blow, and his skull is broken.
The cobbler and the doctor stand beside the body, talking in low voices. They agree that only the huge blacksmith has the strength to strike such a blow.
Father Brown, who has come to the village to visit his friend Wilfred, arrives at the yard with his umbrella. He says very little, but he looks at everything.
Brown crouches beside the body and picks out a small hammer from among the tools. He wonders aloud why so big a man as the blacksmith would use so small a hammer for such a blow.
The police inspector arrives and speaks sharply to the people in the yard. Simeon Barnes, who has just come home from Greenford, is arrested at the gate.
Two men from Greenford come forward and swear that the blacksmith spent the whole night at a prayer meeting. They say that many people saw him there, so he cannot be the killer.
The doctor whispers to Wilfred that the blacksmith's wife may be guilty. She is sitting on a bench near the gate, weeping, with her red hair falling over her face.
Brown, who has overheard, tells the doctor gently that no woman could possibly have struck such a blow. The skull was broken by a force far beyond a woman's arm, he says.
Wilfred suggests, a little too eagerly, that Mad Joe might have done it in some fit of madness. Brown says gently that this theory is not true, and Wilfred turns quickly away.
The doctor is puzzled, because every theory has failed. He turns to Father Brown and asks, rather crossly, whether the priest has any better idea.
The blacksmith, who has been silent, speaks at last in a deep, slow voice. He says that no creature of flesh and blood held that hammer, and that the blow came from heaven.
The villagers murmur among themselves, and some are half inclined to believe him. The doctor shrugs and the inspector scowls, but Wilfred stares at the ground.
Brown draws the doctor aside and gives him two hints. The first is that this is a matter of physical science, and the second is that a flying hammer is nearest the truth.
The doctor frowns and puzzles over the hints, but he cannot find the answer. His eyes wander up to the church tower above the roofs, and then they come down again.
Brown turns to Wilfred and says that he would like to see the church. The curate, who is pale and silent, leads the way up the steep street.
Inside the church Brown asks whether they might go up the tower. The two priests climb the narrow, winding stair, and their footsteps echo on the old stone.
