At the top they step out onto a narrow stone gallery. The whole plain lies below them, and the smithy yard looks small and square, far down among the roofs.
Brown speaks quietly about a man he once knew, who loved to pray in high and lonely places. Little by little, he says, the man began to feel that he was God.
Brown remarks that even a small hammer, dropped from such a height, would strike the ground like a bullet. It would need no strong arm, only the long pull of the earth.
Suddenly Wilfred throws one leg over the wall of the gallery, and for a moment he hangs over the great drop. Brown catches him by the collar and pulls him back with surprising strength.
Wilfred sits shaking on the stone floor with his face in his hands. Brown says quietly that he knows what Wilfred did, and that he will tell no one.
Brown tells the story quietly, and there is no blame in his voice. From the gallery Wilfred saw his brother in the yard below, and in a moment of blind anger he let a hammer fall.
Wilfred weeps bitterly, and Brown puts a gentle hand on his shoulder. He says that the anger Wilfred took for holiness was really only pride.
Brown helps Wilfred to his feet and says again that he will tell nobody. The next step, he says, must be Wilfred's own choice, and he will not force it.
They go down the winding stair in silence, round and round, with the light fading above them. At the bottom the church door stands open, and the sunlight pours in from the village.
Wilfred walks slowly down the steep street toward the smithy yard, and Brown follows a little behind him. The villagers step aside as he passes, and no one speaks a single word.
At the gate Wilfred stops in front of the inspector and says in a clear voice that he has something to tell. Then he says plainly that he killed his brother.
The inspector stares at him in amazement, and the villagers gasp aloud. The doctor remembers Brown's hints about a flying hammer and a matter of science, and at last he understands.
The blacksmith is set free at once, and his wife runs to him and puts her arms round him. The village, which was ready to hate him, now stands quiet and ashamed.

Father Brown walks quietly away up the steep street with his umbrella under his arm. Above him the church tower stands over the village in the sunlight, tall and silent, as it has stood for centuries.

The Sign of the Broken Sword begins on a frozen night, in a churchyard under a hard, bright moon. Father Brown and Flambeau, who is now his friend, stand before the great metal tomb of General St Clare.
General St Clare was a national hero, and people from all over England come to see his tomb. They leave wreaths and flowers there, and some of them stand in silence for a long time.
Brown turns to Flambeau and asks a strange question: where does a wise man hide a leaf? Flambeau says that the answer is easy, because a wise man hides it in the forest.
Then Brown asks what the wise man would do if there were no forest. Flambeau cannot answer, and Brown says in a low voice that he would grow one to hide the leaf.
The two friends leave the churchyard and walk along a frozen road through a dark forest. The trees are black and still, and the stars look very near.
As they walk, Brown says that he will tell the story of General St Clare, which every Englishman knows. He asks Flambeau to listen to it as if he had never heard it before.

Brown begins with the war in Brazil, where General St Clare fought against Olivier, a noble and chivalrous leader. At a river called the Black River the general attacked Olivier with a very small force.
The English force was beaten, and General St Clare was captured. Later he was found hanged from a tree, with his own broken sword hung round his neck.
Flambeau says that he knows the tale well, and that it is a sad one but not a mystery. A brave general was beaten by a stronger enemy and hanged by a cruel one.
Brown says that nobody ever asks two questions about the story. Why did a clever general attack with so small a force, and why did the noble Olivier hang a prisoner?
Brown takes a small book from his pocket, a life of the general written by Captain Keith. Captain Keith is engaged to St Clare's daughter, and Brown reads a page by the light of the moon.
The first clue, Brown says, is a line in Keith's book. It says that St Clare was no fool, and that Olivier was no brute, and Brown asks how both can be true.
The second clue is Olivier's own report of the battle. He writes with respect of the English, who fought with great courage to the end.

Flambeau strides ahead through the dark trees, guessing aloud, and he grows more confident with every guess. Perhaps the general feared madness in his family, he says, and wanted to die in battle, and in despair he took his own life.
Brown shakes his head sadly and says that Flambeau's story is a clean one. The truth, he says, is something much worse, and it is not far away.
Brown speaks of Colonel Clancy, an Irish officer who served under St Clare. In his last illness Clancy cried out against a sword and cursed it with his last breath.
Then Brown speaks of Major Murray, a stern officer from Ulster, who was known as a hard and honest man. He died in the war, and his body was brought home and buried in Belfast.
Brown tells of a third man, Espado, a Brazilian spy known as the Vulture. After the war his private papers fell into English hands, and among them was a soldier's diary.
The diary says that the general, riding a white horse, spoke privately with Major Murray in the dark. Afterwards the general gave the order to attack, and nobody saw Murray alive again.
Brown pauses on the road and asks Flambeau what he makes of the clues. Flambeau frowns, and admits that he can see nothing but a few scattered facts.
Brown stops and says that the other half of the broken sword lies in Major Murray's grave in Belfast. Flambeau looks at him in astonishment, because it is the last thing that he expected.
Brown explains that St Clare's sword snapped when he used it, and that the tip stayed in the body of the dead man. It was buried with him, and nobody ever looked for it.
Brown returns to his riddle and says that he has answered it. A man who must hide a dead body will make a field of dead bodies, for that is the forest where it can hide.
To hide the death of one man, the general led his army into a battle that could not be won. At Black River many soldiers died, and one body among them was never noticed.
Brown says that the great and noble St Clare was really a traitor. He had been selling the secrets of his army to the spy Espado for money.
Major Murray, the stern, honest officer, found out about the treachery. When he faced the general with it, St Clare killed him in a sudden panic, and the sword snapped in the wound.
At dawn the general gave the order to attack with his small force, knowing that it must fail. The soldiers obeyed him without a word, because they believed that he was the bravest of men.
On the hot hill the English soldiers fight until they can fight no more. The few who survive turn their faces toward their white-haired general, and slowly they begin to understand.

In their anger the surviving officers hanged the general from a tree, and they hung the broken blade round his neck. They agreed to tell the world that the enemy had done it, so that the honour of the army would be saved.
The officers made a solemn promise never to tell the truth, for the sake of England's honour. Years later, when Clancy was dying, the memory of that night made him curse the sword.
Flambeau walks on without speaking for a long time. The great hero of England has turned out to be a thief and a murderer, and the thought is hard for him.
At last Flambeau asks whether anyone could prove the story. Brown says that nobody can, because the only proof is a piece of steel in a grave in Belfast.
Flambeau asks what they should do with the secret. Brown says that the general's daughter is going to marry Captain Keith, and that the truth would break her heart.
Brown says that nobody innocent will be blamed if they keep the secret. The general paid for his crime long ago, and the officers who hanged him have suffered for it too.
Flambeau nods slowly and agrees that they should keep the secret. They walk on together until the trees begin to thin and the end of the forest is near.
Far ahead a warm yellow light shines against the frost. It is the window of the inn where they mean to spend the night, and it looks very welcoming.
They come to the door of the inn and look up. Above it hangs a painted sign with a broken sword, and the name of the inn is the Sign of the Broken Sword.
They go inside, where a fire burns in a wide hearth and a few villagers sit at a long table. The two friends take the best seats near the fire and call for something hot to drink.

Flambeau, warming his hands, asks how Brown can understand crime so well. Brown answers quietly that he has heard so many confessions that he knows how evil thinks, though he hopes that he never does it himself.
They sit side by side by the fire, the huge man and the small priest, while the frost whitens the windows. The secret is safe with them, and outside the broken sword swings in the wind.
C1C2: The steamer from the Continent edged against the pier at Harwich in the thin light of an English morning, and the passengers began to stream down the gangway in a noisy, jostling crowd. Among them walked a man whom nobody noticed, a neat and rather quiet figure in plain holiday clothes who seemed to have nothing in the world to hide. It was the beginning of the story called The Blue Cross, and of a chase that was to cross the whole of London.

The quiet man was Aristide Valentin, the head of the Paris police and the most celebrated investigator in the world, whose name was spoken with respect in every capital of Europe. He wore the plain, rather shabby clothes of a man on holiday, and he carried a small bag that gave nothing away. Only a very sharp eye could have seen how carefully he watched each face as it passed him on the pier.

Beneath the loose holiday coat a loaded revolver lay against his ribs, and beside it, folded small, was the card that proved him an officer of the law. Valentin was not on holiday at all, but on the business that had filled his thoughts for weeks. He had crossed the sea to make the greatest arrest of the century, and he meant to make it with his own hands.

His prize was Flambeau, a thief of gigantic size and bottomless cunning, who for years had made a laughing-stock of the police of Europe. Flambeau loved a joke at least as much as he loved a jewel, and his best tricks were told over coffee in every café of Paris. To catch such a man would be the crown of any career, and Valentin knew that he might never be given a second chance.

Flambeau had vanished from France, and every sign told Valentin that the thief had crossed to England, where a great gathering of priests from many nations was about to open in London. Crowds, relics and the costly gifts of the faithful were just what such a man could not resist. It was a thin trail, but it was the only one that the French police possessed.

Of the whole hunt Valentin had one fact to hold on to, and it was a simple one, for Flambeau was enormously tall. A man may change his coat, his voice, his name and even the shape of his face, but he cannot easily make himself shorter by wishing it. Valentin therefore meant to look at every tall man in London and to leave the rest to the thief's own pride.

The train drew out of the town and ran through flat, pale fields toward London, and Valentin gave himself to his task like a hunter at a water-hole. At every station he studied the new passengers as they climbed in, noting their height, their hands and the way they sat down. Nobody escaped him, and nobody satisfied him, for the one man he wanted seemed to be missing from the whole of Essex.

He considered a tall farmer with a red neck, a tall railway guard who was proud of his height, and a lean labourer who stooped as he shuffled along the platform. Each in turn proved to be exactly what he appeared to be, a plain man with plain affairs and no more cunning than his boots. Valentin crossed them off in his mind, one after another, with the patience of a man who has done this many times.

The only traveller who remained was a short priest from the Essex marshes, who sat in the corner with a round, placid face and eyes as mild as milk. Around his feet lay several brown paper parcels that he could not seem to keep together, and a huge, shabby umbrella kept sliding from his knee to the floor. Valentin glanced at him once and thought that here, surely, was the least dangerous creature in all England.

At the next jolt the umbrella slid to the floor once more, and the priest scrambled after it with a worried little cry, scattering two of his parcels in the process. Valentin watched this small disaster with the faint amusement of a man who has seen too many clever faces to be impressed by a stupid one. He dismissed the priest from his thoughts at once, as one dismisses a cloud, and turned again to the window and the flat green country.

In a small, shy voice the priest let it be known that one of his many parcels contained a silver cross set with blue sapphires, an ancient treasure of his church. He was carrying it to London to show to the great gathering of priests, and he spoke of it as another man might speak of his grandmother's teapot. Valentin listened politely, noticing nothing but the dullness of the little man's talk and the foolish way in which he hugged his parcels.

Valentin leaned forward with a polite smile and warned the priest that London was full of clever thieves, and that a cross of such value ought to be guarded closely. The priest thanked him gently and replied that he had his own way of looking after it, a remark that sounded like nothing more than modesty. It was a remark that Valentin would remember with great respect before the day was over, though he thought nothing of it then.

At Liverpool Street the train sighed to a stop and the doors flew open, and a flood of travellers poured out among porters, trolleys and shouting voices. The little priest drifted away into the crowd with his parcels and his umbrella, and in a moment he was no more to be seen than a pebble in a stream. Valentin scarcely noticed the loss, for his mind was already searching the platform for a tall man.

Valentin stood alone on the steps of the station, among cabs and newsboys and hurrying clerks, and admitted to himself that he had no clue at all. His careful method of watching for height had produced nothing, and the thief he was hunting might be anywhere in a city of millions. For the first time on the whole journey he felt the full weight of his task.

Then he did what the French police seldom do, and abandoned his method for a hunch. A thief in disguise, he reasoned, can hide his face and his name but not the strangeness that clings to his actions, and wherever Flambeau had passed there must lie some small thing out of place. He would therefore walk the streets of London and follow whatever seemed wrong, and trust that the wrongness would lead him on.

He walked for a long time through grey, quiet streets, looking into windows and doorways, until the hunt had left him as hungry as it had left him empty-handed. In a still corner near Victoria he came upon a small restaurant with striped blinds, a place so ordinary that he almost walked past it. He went in, chose a table by the wall and sat down with the sigh of a man who has been on his feet since dawn.

He ordered a cup of coffee and, with the absent-mindedness of long habit, stirred in a spoonful of sugar from the bowl on the table. One mouthful told him that the white powder was salt, and a glance at the salt-cellar showed that it was filled with sugar. The thing was so small and so strange that Valentin put down his spoon and began, for the first time that day, to hope.

Valentin called the waiter, who came across the room, looked at the bowl and the cellar, and stared at them with an honest astonishment that could not have been acted. The man swore that both had been in their right places that morning, and then, slowly, his face changed as he remembered the two clergymen who had sat at this very table. They had gone only a little while before, he added, and they had seemed in no hurry at all.

The waiter pointed to a dark stain on the wall opposite the door, where a splash of soup had dried and run down the paper. One of the two clergymen, he explained, had calmly picked up his plate and thrown the soup across the room, and then he had paid his bill as though nothing in the world had happened. Valentin looked from the wall to the waiter and back again, and a slow smile crossed his face.

The clergymen had left only a few minutes before, said the waiter, and had gone up the road in the direction of the shops. Valentin threw some coins on the table, left his coffee untouched, and ran out into the street with a speed that astonished everyone who saw him. For the first time since Harwich he felt like what he was, a hunter who has crossed a fresh track.

A few streets farther on he came to a greengrocer's stall, bright with oranges and heaped with nuts, and the sight stopped him like a hand on his collar. The label that should have stood over the nuts was planted in the oranges, and the label meant for the oranges stood proudly among the nuts. It was the same sort of senseless mischief as the salt and the sugar, and Valentin felt his heart quicken.

The greengrocer, a red-faced man with his sleeves rolled up, was waving his arms at the street and shouting that a clergyman had sent a whole pyramid of his apples rolling into the road. The other clergyman, he admitted more calmly, had paid him for the damage, but a man did not expect such things to happen on a quiet street. When Valentin asked which way the two had gone, he flung out an arm and pointed up the road.

At the corner stood a policeman, large, slow and helpful, who remembered the two clergymen very well, for one of them had been carrying a great umbrella. They had climbed onto a yellow bus, he said, a few minutes earlier, and the bus was bound for Hampstead. Valentin thanked him, showed his card, and in a moment the policeman and a second constable who stood by were ready to follow.

The next yellow bus came rattling up the hill, and Valentin swung himself onto the top deck with the two policemen behind him, where they sat in a row like three travellers on holiday. The seats were hard and the wind was cold, but he cared nothing for the discomfort, for he had found a trail and meant to keep it. From the top of the bus he could see into every shop window and every upstairs room along the road.

The bus laboured north through street after street of shops and chimneys, past churches, public houses and gardens that grew greener as they climbed. Valentin sat very still with his eyes moving from window to window, like a man reading a page of small print, and the two policemen beside him wondered silently what they were meant to be looking for. He himself could have given no reason, but he was certain that the thing he wanted would announce itself.

Then Valentin sprang to his feet, for in the window of a restaurant on the right a single pane of glass had been smashed, leaving a great star-shaped hole with cracks like the rays of a sun. He rang the bell, stopped the bus, and was down in the road with the two policemen at his heels before the conductor could say a word. This was no accident of the road, he told himself, but another signature in the same hand.

Inside, an anxious cashier was counting coins at a little desk beside the damaged window. A clergyman had struck the glass with the point of his umbrella, he explained, and had paid for the damage at once, in exact coins, and then walked out as calmly as he had come in. Valentin listened with growing certainty, for here was the third sign in the same hand, and the hand was leading him northward.

The bus carried them on until the houses fell away and the great green sweep of Hampstead Heath opened before them under a sky that was turning gold. Valentin jumped down and gazed across the grass, the gorse and the winding paths, but the two clergymen were nowhere in sight. There was only a small shop at the edge of the road, with a bright window full of sweets.

In the little sweet shop a woman with a kind, tired face remembered the two clergymen perfectly, for one of them had left a brown paper parcel on her counter by mistake. The short clergyman, she said, had asked her to post it to an address in Westminster, and she had sent it off within the hour. Then she nodded toward the Heath, where the pair had walked away together as the light began to fail.

Valentin looked where she pointed, and far across the slope of the Heath he saw two small dark figures walking side by side against the gold of the sunset, the one tall and the other short. He called the policemen to him, said a few quiet words, and set off across the grass at a pace that was somewhere between a walk and a run. The hunt was no longer in the dark, and the end of it was very near.

The Heath lay wide and empty under a sky streaked with red and gold, and the shadows of the thorn bushes were growing long on the grass. Valentin and the two policemen followed the clergymen at a careful distance, bending low and darting from bush to bush like children playing hide-and-seek. The two black figures never looked back, and they walked on with the unhurried air of men going to church.

At last the pair came to a hollow in the hill, where an old wooden bench stood under the dark mass of a clump of trees, and there they sat down together. One was short and round, the other was tall, and both were black shapes against the glowing sky. Valentin crept up through the bushes behind them until he could hear every word, with the policemen breathing hard at his shoulder.

The detectives lay flat among the roots and the dead leaves, scarcely daring to breathe, and strained their ears toward the bench. What they heard surprised them, for the two clergymen were not plotting a crime but talking in low, calm voices about reason and about heaven. Valentin felt a faint disappointment, as if he had come to a battle and found a debating society.

The short priest gazed up at the first stars and said, in a mild and rather dreamy voice, that reason was always reasonable, even in the last borderlands of the universe. Whatever lay beyond the farthest planet, he went on, it could not be a place where truth stopped being true. He spoke as simply as a child reciting a lesson, and Valentin could hardly believe that this was the man who had led him such a dance.

The tall priest shifted on the bench and answered, with a careless air, that nobody could be certain about worlds so remote. Perhaps, he suggested, there were distant places where reason was a stranger and two and two might make five, and as he said it he stopped, as though he had heard his own words too late. Brown said nothing, but his round face turned toward his companion with an expression of grave attention.

The tall priest rose slowly to his feet, and against the red sky he looked as huge as a tower. In a voice that was suddenly different, light and mocking and perfectly pleased, he announced that he was Flambeau, and that he had swapped the little priest's parcel for one of his own while the other was not looking. He drew a brown paper parcel from his coat and held it out in his enormous hand, as a conjuror shows the card he has just stolen.

The little priest did not leap up, nor cry out, nor even move his hand toward the umbrella that lay against his knee, and his round face stayed as peaceful as a pond. He looked up at the giant and asked mildly whether Flambeau was quite sure that he had taken the right parcel. There was something so innocent and so patient in the question that the thief hesitated, and for the first time a shadow crossed his triumph.

Flambeau ripped the string apart with his great hands, tore the brown paper open, and stared at what lay inside. There was no cross, no silver and no blue stones, but only a lump of dull lead and a few sheets of crumpled paper, such as any child might have packed. For a moment the thief stood perfectly still, and the colour drained slowly out of his bold face.

Brown told him gently that he had watched the parcels being changed, and that he had quietly changed them back again. The real cross was already on its way to Westminster, he said, left with a kind woman in a sweet shop, and the salt, the apples and the broken window were his own small trail. He explained that he had laid it so that someone in authority would be bound to follow, and he said this with a faint apology, as a man might who has accidentally stepped on a friend's foot.

Flambeau asked in a hollow voice how Brown had known that he was no true priest, and Brown replied that the stranger had attacked reason, and that this is bad theology. At that moment Valentin and his two policemen stepped out of the trees, and in a few seconds the great thief, who was still holding his empty parcel, found himself arrested and his career at an end. Valentin turned to the little priest from Essex and bowed to him very low, with the grave respect that one expert pays to another.

The Queer Feet begins in Belgravia, in the glow of lamps at evening, at the Vernon Hotel, one of those small and very grand places that charge a great deal and say very little. Its owner, Mr Lever, was a stiff, careful man who valued the hotel's good name above everything, and he watched his waiters as a general watches his troops. On this particular night he had more reason than usual to be careful, for the hotel was giving a dinner.

Mr Lever walked slowly through the hall and the dining room, straightening a chair here and a flower there, with the critical eye of a man who has never forgiven a fault. The waiters stood in a neat line, dressed in black coats and white shirts, and he passed along it like an officer inspecting a guard of honour. Everything in the hotel had to be perfect before the first guest arrived, for its reputation rested on such small things.

The guests were the members of a club called the Twelve True Fishermen, a very select society that held its dinner once a year in the same hotel and in the same room. They arrived one by one in black evening dress, grave, well fed and rather pleased with themselves, and they greeted one another as men greet in a church. The whole business was done with ceremony, and no one would have dreamed of hurrying it.

The chairman of the evening was Mr Audley, a dignified man who took the whole business very seriously, and beside him stood the young Duke of Chester, the club's vice-president, who was well liked and rather amused by it all. A little apart from them stood Colonel Pound, a stiff and silent member who said nothing and seemed to disapprove of everything. These were the three gentlemen on whom the success of the evening was supposed to depend.

In the private dining room above the garden the long table was laid for twelve, and the silver gleamed under the lamps like the scales of a great fish. The pride of the club was its set of twelve silver fish knives and forks, each one set with pearls, which were laid out for this dinner every year. The waiters had been told to handle them as they would handle the crown jewels.

The waiters glided around the table in their black coats and white shirts, and in the lamplight they were scarcely to be told from the gentlemen they served. It is one of the curious facts of social life that the evening dress of a rich man and the working dress of his waiter are almost exactly alike. Nobody in the room gave this the smallest thought, which was just what was going to make it important.

While these preparations went forward, a small, shabby figure in black came to a side door of the hotel, carrying a large umbrella and looking as if he had walked a long way. It was Father Brown, who had been sent for by one of the waiters, an old man who had been struck down by a sudden illness upstairs and had asked, with great earnestness, to see a priest. He gave his name humbly at the door and was shown in without any fuss.

Upstairs, in a bare little room, Father Brown sat beside the sick waiter's bed and listened to him with great kindness and no sign of hurry. When the old man had said all that he needed to say, the priest rose quietly, left him to rest, and came down the stairs to write a note that he had promised to put on paper. He was a man who never thought that any task was too small, nor any person too humble.

Mr Lever, who dreaded the thought of a shabby priest being seen by his grand guests, hurried to meet him in the passage and hid him away. He shut Brown into a small room that lay between the glass office and the cloakroom, and told him that he might write there in peace. The little priest thanked him with perfect good humour and sat down at a table with a pen.

The room was small and rather dim, with a narrow window and a table pushed into one corner, and there Brown sat down alone with his pen and a sheet of the hotel's paper. The door stood a little open to the passage outside, and through it came the clatter of plates, the murmur of voices, and the distant, cheerful noise of a great dinner beginning. He bent over his note and began to write, a very small figure in a very quiet corner.

As he wrote, the priest became aware of footsteps in the passage outside, and they were of the strangest kind. A swift, light run passed the door, followed after a pause by a slow and heavy stamp, as of a man who has nothing in the world to do, and then the swift run began again. Brown raised his head and listened, with his head a little on one side, like a bird that has heard a curious sound in the grass.

The sounds came again and again, always in the same strange order, and each time the passage gave out the same faint creak at the same place. Brown laid down his pen and listened as he might have listened to a puzzle in music, counting the beats of the swift steps and the beats of the slow ones. Something about them troubled him deeply, though he could not yet say what it was.

The priest decided that the slow steps belonged to an idle gentleman strolling at his ease, one of the wealthy diners perhaps, with a good dinner before him and nothing on his mind. The swift, soft steps were different, for they were the steps of a man in a hurry who does not wish to be heard, and they reminded Brown of something that he could not quite place. He frowned at the ceiling, and the pen stopped moving in his hand, for the odd sounds in the passage had begun to haunt him.

Brown went out of his little room and found, on the other side of the empty cloakroom counter, a tall and elegant man in perfect evening dress, who asked in a clear, bright voice for his hat and coat. He explained that he was in a great hurry, and he threw down half a sovereign upon the counter as though the matter were settled. Brown looked at the coin, and then at the man, and said in his gentle voice that the gentleman must have silver in his pocket.

In an instant the man had vaulted over the counter and seized the little priest by the collar, with a face that was no longer elegant and no longer smiling. Brown did not struggle or cry out, but said gravely that he was a priest, that he was not afraid, and that he was quite ready, if the gentleman wished it, to hear his confession. The words fell into the dim, quiet room like a stone into a pond.

The thief released him, took a step backward, and sank slowly into a chair, staring at the priest as if he had seen the very face of fate. All the colour had gone out of his handsome cheeks, and his great hands lay open on his knees like the hands of a child who has been caught. He did not speak, for there was nothing in his long experience of crime that could have prepared him for this little man in the dim room.

Meanwhile, in the dining room above the garden, the members of the club made a discovery that struck them dumb. The plates of the fish course had been taken away by a waiter, and with them had gone every one of the twelve silver knives and forks, the whole pearl-handled treasure of the club. When Mr Lever was fetched, he declared in a shaking voice that he had never sent that waiter at all.

Mr Audley rose at the head of the long table and announced the loss in a voice that trembled with outrage, while the Duke of Chester sat open-mouthed and Colonel Pound stared ahead like a stone man. The waiters were summoned and questioned one by one, and each swore that he knew nothing of the man who had taken the plates. It dawned on the company by slow degrees that a thief had walked among them in a waiter's coat, and had served them with his own hands.

Brown told the thief quietly that he had understood the footsteps, for the slow steps and the swift steps had been one man's, a gentleman's and a waiter's, and the same black clothes had served for both. The thief looked at him for a long moment, laughed softly, and drew the silver out of his pockets and laid it gleaming on the counter. Then, with one bound, he burst out through the window and was lost in the darkness of the garden.

The members crowded into the cloakroom, and there on the counter lay the silver, bright and whole, beside the burst window with its frame hanging in splinters. Brown explained mildly that one man had played both the gentleman and the waiter, and that nobody had noticed because their evening dress was the same. The Twelve True Fishermen, who disliked being fooled, resolved that in future they would wear green coats, so that no thief could ever again be mistaken for a waiter.

The Flying Stars begins on Boxing Day, the morning after Christmas, in a frosty garden on the edge of Putney, where the bare branches stood out like iron against the pale sky. A young girl named Ruby Adams was scattering crumbs for the birds with a quick, generous hand. She had the pink cheeks and light movements of a creature who loves the cold.

Suddenly a young man swung himself over the garden wall and dropped down on the frozen grass in front of her, scattering the birds in every direction. He was John Crook, a young journalist with untidy hair and a restless way of talking, and he was very much in love with Ruby. He had been waiting on that wall, it seemed, for most of the morning.

Crook was a Socialist of the most earnest kind, and even on Boxing Day morning he could not stop talking about the wrongs of the poor and the follies of the rich. Ruby listened with a smile that was half amusement and half affection, for she liked him better than she would admit. She told him that her father, the silent old Colonel Adams, was expecting an important guest that very day.

A green motor car came up the drive with a noise like a small thunderstorm and stopped at the gate, and servants ran out to help the passenger. Out of a great heap of furs there emerged Sir Leopold Fischer, Ruby's rich godfather, who was old, stiff and extremely pleased with his own importance. He blinked at the winter garden like a man who has not been out of doors for years.

On the steps of the house three men stood waiting to welcome the guest, and they made a curious group. There was the silent Colonel Adams, the master of the house, a bright and cheerful man named James Blount who had lately come from Canada, and Father Brown, small, round and shabby, holding his umbrella like a staff. Sir Leopold nodded to them all with an air of kindly condescension, as a king might nod to his humbler subjects.

In the warm, firelit hall Sir Leopold drew a flat case from the pocket of his coat with the air of a conjuror, and held it up for the whole company to see. He told Ruby, in his dry, pompous voice, that this was her Christmas present from a godfather who had never been known to be generous by halves. Everyone drew close, and even the Colonel took his pipe out of his mouth.

He pressed a catch and the case sprang open, and on a bed of orange velvet three enormous diamonds blazed up in the firelight like a small, captive sun. They were African stones, and they were known throughout the world as the Flying Stars, a name earned by their habit of being stolen almost as often as they were sold. Ruby gave a little cry of wonder, and even Crook, who despised all such display, fell silent for a moment.

Sir Leopold held one of the great stones up to the light and told the company, with a pleasure that was not quite free of vanity, how thieves had followed the diamonds from owner to owner for years. He declared with a dry laugh that he himself was in no danger, for he kept them always about his person. The colonel grunted, Ruby clapped her hands, and Father Brown, who had hardly spoken, looked at the case with his head on one side.

Crook, who could never resist a speech, remarked that such wealth locked in one small case was a scandal in a world where so many went hungry. Sir Leopold drew himself up and frowned, and from that moment he looked at the young journalist as a man looks at a dog that may bite. Ruby blushed and the Colonel coughed, but Father Brown only smiled at the fire.

At that moment a dusty messenger appeared at the open front door with a letter for Mr Blount, who tore it open and read it with growing delight. His round, cheerful face lit up like a lamp, and he looked from the letter to the company as though he had been given a present too. Whatever news the letter held, it was clearly going to change the plans for the day.

He waved the letter above his head and announced that it came from his old friend Florian, the famous French acrobat and comic actor, who was coming to visit them that very night. Blount was as excited as a schoolboy let out of class, and he walked up and down the hall rubbing his hands. It seemed to the company that the whole evening had been rearranged in a moment.

Blount cried that nothing could be more fitting than a Christmas pantomime in the hall, in the good old English way, with no more than a few hours to prepare. He cast himself as the harlequin, Crook as the clown, Ruby as the columbine and the colonel as the pantaloon, and he gave out the parts with the air of a general giving orders. Nobody dared to object, for no one in that house could resist his cheerfulness, and the colonel only shrugged and smiled.

He ran to the telephone, spoke for a minute in a rapid, laughing voice, and returned to say that Florian would bring a policeman's costume and play the part of the constable himself. At once the whole house was in motion, with servants running for cardboard, paint and old curtains, and the hall slowly changing into a stage. Brown watched the whirl of preparation with his usual mild interest, like a man at a fair.

The actors covered themselves with silver paper, white flour and paste jewels until they glittered like Christmas trees, and the hall was full of dazzling strangers who could scarcely be told apart. Crook rubbed flour on his face for the clown's white mask, Ruby tied ribbons in her hair, and the colonel put on a long nightcap and a ridiculous nose. Only Brown remained plainly himself, and seemed rather out of place among the glitter.

Blount, in the highest of spirits, pushed a paper donkey's head over Father Brown's round face, and the priest wore it with perfect good humour, blinking mildly through the eyeholes. Then he skipped across to Sir Leopold and pretended to pin a long paper tail on the back of his coat, to the great delight of the servants. Sir Leopold, who disliked being made a fool of, stiffened like a poker and said nothing.

By evening the great hall had been turned into a little theatre, with a rough curtain hung across one end and rows of chairs set out in the lamplight. Servants, neighbours and the children of the village crowded the benches, and in the front row sat Sir Leopold, wrapped in his furs and as upright as a monument. At last the curtain trembled, a bell rang somewhere behind it, and the pantomime began amid a burst of eager applause.

The pantomime began with a wild chase, for Crook the clown tumbled across the stage with the pantaloon at his heels, tripping over everything and everyone. The audience laughed until the benches shook, and even Sir Leopold allowed himself a thin, grudging smile. Ruby danced in as the columbine, light as a feather, and the applause grew louder still.

Then came the harlequin, glittering from head to foot, who danced across the stage, knocked the policeman flat with a touch of his wand, and tossed him about like a sack of flour. The audience roared, for the unfortunate constable seemed to have no bones at all, and he flopped from one side of the stage to the other with the helplessness of a rag doll. It was, everyone agreed afterwards, the best part of the whole performance, and the children begged for it to be done again.

When the curtain fell, the whole hall burst into clapping and cheering, and the actors bowed again and again from behind it. But Sir Leopold had risen to his feet, and his face, which had been so stiff and calm, was changing as he felt anxiously through every pocket of his coat. The applause died away in a puzzled silence, and the actors looked at one another from behind the curtain, wondering what was wrong.

He cried out in a strangled voice that the diamonds had vanished from his pocket, and he strode out of the hall with a face as white as paper. The cheerful noise of the evening stopped as if a door had been shut upon it, and the guests stared at one another in dismay. Nobody seemed to know whether to follow him or to stay where they were.

In the study Sir Leopold declared that the stones had been stolen under his very nose, while he sat peacefully watching the play. The colonel stood before him in his white paint and his absurd nightcap, trying to calm him with gruff and clumsy words, and looking more ridiculous than he had ever done on the stage. The guests crowded at the door, and the old man looked slowly from face to face.

Sir Leopold stretched out a shaking finger toward Crook, whom he had disliked from the first, and declared that the Socialist was the thief. Crook turned out every pocket of his clown's costume and found them empty, and Father Brown observed gently that the man who steals diamonds is not often the man who makes speeches about the poor. He added that it would be wiser to look for someone whom the house did not know.

Everyone joined in the search, and the house was turned upside down, from the stairs and the cupboards to the ruined paper scenery on the stage. They found paste jewels, torn ribbons and one lost slipper, but there was no sign of the Flying Stars anywhere. By now the glitter of the evening had faded, and the hall looked like the morning after a fair.

In all the confusion nobody had noticed that the policeman was still lying on the stage exactly where the harlequin had dropped him, one arm flung out and his helmet rolled aside. Father Brown, whose quick eyes missed little, went up the steps and bent over him in the lamplight. The man had not moved since the curtain fell, and his chest rose and fell very slowly.

Brown turned to the colonel and asked him quietly when Mrs Adams had died, and the old soldier answered that it was a week before Blount had arrived from Canada. Blount had come, it seemed, to visit an old friend of the family, and had found that he was too late. Brown nodded slowly, and he glanced across the hall at the cheerful man in the glittering costume.

A sweet, sickly smell hung about the man's face, and Brown, who had met it before in the course of his work, recognised it at once as chloroform. The policeman had not been acting at all, for he had been drugged before the pantomime ever began, and he had lain senseless through the whole of the performance. It was the first solid fact in a mystery that had so far consisted only of absences.

While the household argued and searched, Father Brown slipped away through the garden door into the cold brilliance of the moonlight. He crossed the frozen lawn with his umbrella under his arm, a small black figure on the silver grass, and made his way toward the dark mass of the trees. He seemed to know exactly where he was going, though nobody had told him.

High in the branches of a bare tree something was glittering like frost, and Brown looked up at it without any sign of surprise. It was a man in a costume of silver paper, crouched among the twigs with the moonlight running down his glittering sleeves, and Brown knew him at once for the thief Flambeau. He was hiding, as the cleverest of thieves hide, in the one place where nobody had thought to look.

Brown spoke up to him gently, with a little praise for the plot, which had used a false old friend, a Christmas pantomime and a drugged policeman, and which was as neat as a well-made watch. Then he begged the thief to give back the stones, and to give up his dangerous trade while he was still young enough to give it up. He said that it was a fine thing to be clever, but a finer thing to be good, and he said it without the smallest trace of reproach.

For a long moment there was no answer, and then something sparkled in the moonlight and fell from the tree into the frozen grass, and another sparkle followed, and then a third. The silver figure dropped lightly to the ground, bowed once to the little priest, and was swallowed up by the shadows of the garden. It was the last crime that Flambeau ever committed, and the beginning of a very different life.

The Invisible Man opens in Camden Town, in a long street of small shops where the light of the morning fell in thin gold lines across the pavement. A young Scottish artist named John Turnbull Angus, with red hair and an excited face, walked briskly up to a sweet shop whose window was full of cakes and sugared fruit. He had made up his mind about something, and nothing was going to stop him.

He sat down at a small table by the window and ordered a bun and a cup of coffee, in the voice of a man who has no interest whatever in either. The girl who served him was Laura Hope, quick and graceful, and it was for her sake alone that he had walked so far. She set down the cup with a quiet smile and waited, as if she already knew what was coming.

He laid down his spoon, looked up at her and said, in plain words and without any of the flourishes he had prepared, that he loved her and wished her to marry him. Laura stood perfectly still beside the table, holding the empty tray against her apron, and for a long moment she did not seem to breathe. In the shop the clock ticked loudly, and a fly buzzed against the window as if it, too, were waiting for her answer.

Laura said gently that she liked him better than anyone she knew, but that she could give him no answer until he had heard her story. She sat down opposite him with her hands folded in her lap, like a child about to recite, and her face was grave and a little sad. Angus waited with his heart beating, ready to listen to anything she wished to tell.

She told him that she came from the small town of Ludbury, in a quiet corner of the country where nothing much ever happened. But two suitors there, in the space of a single summer, had courted her with equal ardour, and she had never been able to banish either of them from her thoughts. They were as unlike each other, she said, as two men could possibly be, and that was the strange part of the whole affair.

The first was Isidore Smythe, a small, neat man with a head full of ideas and a pair of wonderfully clever hands. He had invented clockwork servants that could do the work of real ones, and the world had paid him so much for them that he was now a millionaire. In those days, Laura remembered, he had been poor, and nobody in Ludbury had dreamed how far he would go.

The other was James Welkin, a tall man with a terrible squint and a quiet, hungry way of looking at her, though nobody could say at which eye he looked. She had never liked him, and as the summer went on she had come to fear him, though she could not have said exactly why. Gentle as she was, she had refused him more than once, and he had never forgotten it.

Laura had refused them both, since she loved neither, and she had hoped, with the simple optimism of a girl, that they would forget her and find happiness elsewhere. But Smythe had grown rich and ambitious, and Welkin had vanished into the world and left a cold shadow behind him. She could not feel certain that either story had really ended, and the doubt lay on her like a cold hand.

Welkin had gone away long ago, said Laura, and no one in Ludbury had ever learned where he went, but lately she had had an uneasy feeling that he was somewhere close, watching and waiting. She could not explain it, and she felt a little ashamed to mention it, for there was nothing to prove that the feeling was more than a fancy. Angus took her hand across the table and told her, with great firmness, that while he lived she would be safe.

Just as she reached the end of her story, the shop door opened with a bang and a small man in a top hat came hurrying in, with a car waiting at the kerb behind him. Laura gave a little gasp and half rose from her chair, for the visitor was none other than Isidore Smythe, the millionaire of whom she had been speaking. He looked at her with burning eyes, and then at the young man opposite her, and his face grew pale.

Smythe pointed with a trembling finger at a long strip of paper that had been pasted across the shop window, in thin, neat handwriting. It said, as plainly as words could say it, that if Laura ever married Smythe, then Smythe would die. Laura stared at it with her hand at her throat, and nobody spoke for a long moment.

Smythe explained in a thin, shaking voice that this was not the first warning, for five threatening letters had already come to him at his flat, each saying that he would die if he persisted in his hopes. Nobody had seen who brought them, and the porter swore that no stranger had come near the door. He was a clever man, but he was a frightened one, and he did not pretend otherwise.

Angus, who was brave and not a little jealous, declared that he would go with Smythe at once and see these famous letters for himself. Laura begged them both to be careful, and her eyes followed the little car as it drove away. It was an odd pair of rivals who sat side by side that morning, the red-haired young artist and the small anxious millionaire, united by a common danger.

The little car climbed a steep road beyond the canal, up to Himylaya Mansions, a tall block of flats that stood on the hill like a great ship on a green wave. At the entrance a doorman in a coat covered with gold braid stood stiffly at attention, while a porter polished brass inside. Smythe lived at the very top, and the lift carried the two men upward in silence.

The flat was filled with clockwork servants, standing in rows along the walls like a silent army, and not one of them had been given a head. Smythe built them there himself, and in the bright, empty rooms the sight was strange enough to send a shiver down the spine. Angus walked among them like a man in a dream, half expecting that one of them might turn and speak.

Among the rows of headless figures Angus found a scrap of paper lying on the floor, written in red ink and in the same neat handwriting as the strip in the window. It threatened Smythe in the same cold words, and nobody could say how it had come into a flat that had been shut while its owner was out. Smythe stared at it for a long moment, and the colour left his face, so that he looked like one of his own pale figures.

Angus decided that Smythe needed more than a young artist to protect him, and that he knew exactly where to find it. His friend Flambeau, once the most famous thief in Europe, had long ago given up crime and become a private detective, and he would be the very man for such a puzzle. Angus promised to fetch him at once, and Smythe, who was pale with fear, agreed.

Before leaving, Angus took every precaution, for he paid a porter, the doorman, a policeman across the street and an old chestnut seller to watch the building and to let him know if anyone went in. Then he went down into the street, buttoned his coat against the cold and set off at a brisk pace to find his friend. It was growing dark, and the sky had an odd, heavy look, as if it were holding something back.

Angus hurried to Lucknow Mansions, where Flambeau lived among sabres, pistols and a sleek Persian cat, and found the great man in his shirt sleeves beside the fire. Opposite him sat a small priest in a black coat, whose round face and mild eyes belonged to a man who had seen a great many things and been surprised by none. It was Father Brown, and Flambeau introduced them with a wave of his hand.

Angus poured out the whole tale, from the sweet shop to the headless servants, while Flambeau listened with the keen interest of an old hunter and Brown sat quietly with his hands on his knees. As he talked, the first flakes of snow began to drift across the window, exactly as the quiet little priest had said that they would. The sky above Camden Town was growing dark and soft, and the lamps in the street were beginning to glow one by one.

Flambeau and Brown agreed at once, and the three men set off through the thickening snow toward Himylaya Mansions, with the white flakes settling on their hats and shoulders. The streets were growing quiet, and the lamps made soft yellow halos in the dusk. Brown walked along with his umbrella under his arm, saying very little and looking at the pavements.

At the building the four watchers still stood at their posts, a little whiter with snow, and each of them swore solemnly that nobody had gone in or out since Angus had left. The porter, the doorman, the policeman and the chestnut seller all said the same, and they said it with the stubbornness of honest men who are not used to being doubted. Angus looked at his friends in bewilderment, for if the four men were honest, then the thing seemed to him quite impossible.

Brown said nothing at first, but bent to look at the doorway, and then he pointed at a line of grey footprints that crossed the new snow within a few inches of the doorman's gold-braided legs. The marks went in at the door and came out again, quite plainly, and yet not one of the four honest watchers had seen the man who made them. It was as if an invisible creature had walked between them in plain view.

They hurried up the stairs and burst into the flat, but Smythe was nowhere to be found, and the headless figures stood in their long rows as if nothing had happened. On the floor, near the middle of the room, there was a dark stain that had not been there before, and Angus felt his stomach turn cold. The little millionaire had vanished as completely as a coin from a conjuror's hand.

While the others were still staring at the stain, Brown spoke quietly to the policeman and asked him to go and search the streets and the canal at the bottom of the hill. A few minutes later the man came running back through the snow, breathless and pale, to say that the body of Isidore Smythe had been found in the canal, killed by a single stab. Angus stared at him in horror, and Flambeau let out a low whistle, while Brown stood silent and very pale.

Brown asked the policeman, in the same quiet voice, whether anyone had found a light brown sack near the body, and the man stared at him in blank astonishment. Nobody had found one, he said, and he could not imagine why the priest should ask. Brown nodded slowly, as though the answer were exactly the one he had expected, and his eyes went to the snow in the street below.

As the three men walked down the hill through the falling snow, Brown explained, in his quiet and rather apologetic way, that people always answer the question they think is meant, not the question that is asked. The four watchers had honestly meant that nobody unusual had gone in, whereas a man had certainly entered and left, and had been so ordinary that nobody had seen him. The threatening letters, after all, had been carried to Smythe's door by somebody, and there is one man whom every house lets in without a thought.

At the bottom of the hill a postman was trudging through the snow with a heavy bag on his back, and nobody had given him a glance, for the postman is the most familiar sight in the world. Brown stepped up to him and laid a hand lightly on his shoulder, and said a few quiet words that nobody else could hear. The man stopped dead as if he had been struck, and for a moment he did not turn round at all.

The postman turned slowly round, and his face had a terrible squint, so that he seemed to look at two men at once and at neither. He was James Welkin, who had written the threats and delivered them with his own hands, and who had killed Smythe in his flat and carried the body away in his mail bag. Nobody had seen him because everybody had seen him a thousand times, and he had been no more than a part of the street.

Angus turned and ran back through the snow to Laura, to tell her that the danger was over and that she was free to answer his question in peace. Brown and the murderer walked slowly away over the white hills, side by side, the one small and quiet and the other tall and broken, and nobody ever knew all that was said between them. That night the snow fell until the whole of London was silent, and it covered the footprints of the guilty and the innocent alike.

The Hammer of God is set in Bohun Beacon, a village perched on so steep a hill that its cottages seemed to be climbing over one another's roofs to reach the top. At dawn the grey tower of the church stood up above the chimneys, with the pale sky behind it and a few rooks wheeling round its crown. The streets were still empty, and the whole village lay in that deep silence which comes before the first cart.

The blacksmith of the village was Simeon Barnes, a man so huge that the villagers said he could have carried the anvil under one arm, and so grave that he was seldom seen to smile. He was deeply religious in a stern and private way, and it was his habit to walk to the nearby town of Greenford and join the prayer meetings held there. His forge stood in a walled yard behind the cottages, among piles of iron and hammers of every size.

In the grey light of that morning two brothers met in the village street, and no two men could have looked less alike. Colonel Norman Bohun was a wild, wealthy man who feared nothing and lived only for his own pleasure, while his brother Wilfred was a quiet, devout priest whose thin face was pale with sleeplessness. They had never understood one another, and each regarded the other with a mixture of love and impatience.

Norman laughed in his careless way and teased his brother about his long face and his early prayers, but Wilfred, who had passed a sleepless night, answered in a low, earnest voice and begged him to change his ways. He spoke of the soul and of judgement, and the colonel listened with the bright, mocking eyes of a man who has heard it all before. It was one more quarrel in a long family war, and neither of them knew that it was the last.

Then Wilfred grew more urgent and warned his brother about the blacksmith, Simeon Barnes, who had good reason to hate the colonel and was a man of terrible strength. He begged him to keep away from the forge and from all that belonged to the smith, for there are injuries which a quiet man does not forget. The colonel only laughed, and said that a blacksmith was no more to him than a horse to be shod.

Norman declared that he was afraid of no man living, least of all a village smith, and he strolled away down the street whistling, with the sunrise coming gold over the roofs. Wilfred stood looking after him, and his lips moved slightly, as if in prayer or in grief. Then the colonel turned a corner at the bottom of the hill, and the street was empty again, as if he had never been there.

Wilfred, who was the curate of the village church, turned in at its porch and went inside to pray alone. The great building was cold and dim, full of shadows and old stone, and the only sound in it was the wind that whispered in the high tower above him. He knelt, but his thoughts would not be still, and he stayed there for a long time.

In the village street the cobbler Gibbs sat working at his window, tapping at a boot, and watched the morning go by. A simple-minded lad called Mad Joe wandered past, talking to himself and smiling at the sky, as harmless as a child and as much a part of the village as the church tower. Gibbs nodded to him, as he did every morning, and went on tapping at the old boot as though nothing in the world could disturb him.

Not long afterwards the cobbler came running up the street toward the church, with his leather apron flapping and his face the colour of wax. He found Wilfred in the porch and told him, in broken gasps, that the colonel lay dead in the smithy yard, and that the doctor had already been sent for. Wilfred heard him without a word, and the colour drained from his thin face, and then he began to run.

Wilfred ran down the steep street so fast that he almost fell, with the cobbler hurrying behind him and the cottages flying past on either side. At the gate of the smithy yard a small crowd had gathered, villagers in their working clothes, whispering together, and the whispering stopped as he arrived. They parted without a word to let the dead man's brother through, and he went forward alone into the yard.

The colonel lay on his back among the hammers and bars and scraps of iron, with his arms flung wide and his face turned to the sky, and he had been killed by a single terrible blow. The skull had been broken as an eggshell is broken, and yet the rest of the body was untouched, as if the blow had come out of the air. Wilfred stood looking down at him for a long moment, and no one dared to speak.

The cobbler and the doctor stood beside the body and talked together in low voices, and the longer they talked the more certain they became. Only one man in the whole district, they agreed, had the strength to strike so terrible a blow, and that man was Simeon Barnes the blacksmith, whose huge arm had made the iron ring for many years. It was as plain as daylight, said the doctor, and the cobbler nodded his grey head.

Father Brown, who had come to the village that morning to visit his friend Wilfred, arrived at the gate of the yard with his battered umbrella and stood there quietly. He said very little to anyone, but his small grey eyes moved over everything in the yard, the body, the hammers, the walls and the sky, as if he were counting them. Wilfred saw him and was glad, though in that terrible hour he could not have said why he wanted the little priest near him.

Brown crouched among the tools and drew out a small hammer, a mere light thing such as a boy might lift, and turned it over in his hand. He remarked, as if to himself, that it was strange that so huge a man as the blacksmith should choose so small a hammer to do such a deed, when his own great hammers lay close by. Nobody answered him, for nobody present saw what he meant, and the doctor was already talking of something else.

The police inspector arrived from the town, brisk and businesslike, and cleared the yard of whispering villagers. Simeon Barnes, who had just come home from Greenford and had barely time to take in what had happened, was arrested at the gate, and he stood among the officers like an oak among saplings. He said nothing at all, and only looked at the dead man with a face of stone.

Then two men from Greenford came forward, serious and respectable, and swore that the blacksmith had spent the whole night with them at a prayer meeting and had not left the town until the morning was well advanced. Many other people had seen him there, they said, and it would be impossible to find a man in Greenford who would say otherwise. The inspector frowned and scratched his head, for he had been so very sure, and he did not like to lose a good theory.

The doctor drew Wilfred aside and whispered that, since the blacksmith could not have done it, his wife might have done so, for the colonel had caused her much pain. They looked together at the red-haired woman, who sat weeping on a bench by the gate with her hands over her face. She did not look like a murderess, or like anything but a creature who has been ill-used.

Brown, who had overheard, told the doctor in his mild, apologetic voice that no woman could possibly have struck such a blow, for the force needed was far beyond any woman's arm. The doctor, who had been quite pleased with his theory, looked a little hurt, and said that in that case he would be glad to hear a better one. Brown said nothing at all, and looked up at the sky, where the grey tower of the church stood out against the clouds.

Wilfred then suggested, a little too eagerly, that Mad Joe, the simple-minded lad, might have done the deed in some sudden fit of madness. Brown shook his head and told him gently that this theory was not true, and there was something in his tone that made Wilfred turn quickly away. The curate's hands, the others noticed, were trembling like leaves in the wind, and his face was as white as paper.

The doctor was thoroughly puzzled, since every theory in turn had been swept away, and he turned to Father Brown and asked him rather crossly whether he had any better idea of his own. Brown, who had been listening with his head on one side, replied that he had, but that it was a very strange one, and that it was not a matter of men and women at all. The inspector, the doctor and the cobbler stared at him in silence, wondering what a strange little priest could possibly know.

Simeon Barnes, who had stood silent among the officers, spoke at last in a deep and solemn voice that made the whole yard hush. He said that no thing of flesh and blood had held that hammer, that no human arm could have struck such a blow, and that it was a thunderbolt out of heaven that had struck the colonel down. His eyes were wide and shining, and nobody who looked at him doubted for a moment that he believed every word.

The villagers began to murmur among themselves, and some of them were half inclined to believe what the blacksmith said, for there are old tales in every village of men struck down by powers they could not see. The doctor shrugged his shoulders, the inspector scowled and tugged at his moustache, and Wilfred stared at the ground without speaking. Only Father Brown seemed to be listening to something else, with his round face turned a little to one side.

Brown took the doctor aside, under the shadow of the wall, and gave him two small hints in his softest voice. The first was that the matter was one of physical science and not of mystery, and the second was that the story of a flying hammer was nearer to the truth than the doctor imagined. The doctor, who thought himself a man of science, listened with his mouth a little open.

The doctor frowned and puzzled over the two hints for a long time, but he could find no sense in them, for a hammer is a thing that is held and not a thing that flies. His eyes wandered up to the church tower that rose above the roofs of the village, and then back to the dull ground of the yard. Something stirred at the back of his mind, but he could not quite catch it.

Brown turned to Wilfred and said, in a casual way, that he would very much like to see the church, which he had heard was a fine one. The curate, who was pale and strangely silent, nodded and led the way up the steep street, and the two priests walked together without speaking. Behind them the noise of the yard faded, and ahead of them the tower grew taller at every step.

Inside the cold church Brown asked, with childlike interest, whether they might go up the tower for the view, and Wilfred, after a moment's hesitation, agreed. The two priests climbed the narrow, winding stair, round and round in the darkness, and their footsteps echoed on the worn stone like the beating of slow hearts. Light began to appear above them like a pale coin, and the air grew colder and fresher with every turn of the stair.

At the top they stepped out onto a narrow stone gallery that ran round the outside of the tower, and the wind caught at their black coats. The whole plain lay spread beneath them like a map, with its fields and hedges and little white roads, and far down among the cottages was the smithy yard, small and square as a postage stamp. It was a place from which one might see everything, and be seen by nobody.

Brown leaned on the stone and spoke quietly of a man he had once known, who loved to pray in high and lonely places and would climb to the top of any tower or hill to be alone with heaven. Little by little, in some dizzy corner of the spire, the man's brain had turned, and he had come to fancy that he was God, and that the people far below were no more than ants. Wilfred listened with his face as white as the stone, and his hands gripped the rail.

Then Brown remarked, in the same casual voice, that even a small hammer, if it were dropped from such a height as this, would strike the ground below like a bullet from a gun. It would need no huge arm to do such a thing, he said, but only the long and patient pull of the earth. Wilfred made a strange sound in his throat, like a man who is trying not to cry out.

Suddenly Wilfred threw one leg over the parapet, and for a moment he hung above the great void, with the wind in his black coat and his eyes fixed on nothing. The little priest, who had been watching him from the first, caught him by the collar and dragged him back with a strength that nobody would have guessed was in him. They fell together in a heap on the stone floor of the gallery, and for a long moment neither of them moved.

Wilfred sat on the stone floor, shaking from head to foot, with his face hidden in his hands, and for a long time he did not speak. Brown sat down beside him, as gently as a nurse beside a child, and said quietly that he knew what Wilfred had done, and that he would tell nobody. The wind blew over the tower, and the rooks cried above them in the grey air.

In a soft voice that held no blame, Brown told the story as he understood it. From this very gallery Wilfred had seen his brother walking in the smithy yard far below, and in one dreadful moment of blind anger, which he took for holy zeal, he had let a small hammer fall from the tower. It had dropped through the empty air like a thunderbolt, and nobody had seen whence it came.

Wilfred wept bitterly, and Brown laid a gentle hand upon his shoulder and told him that the anger he had taken for holy zeal had been only pride, the dark pride of the man who fancied himself God. It was a hard truth to speak, but it was spoken with such pity that it seemed to heal as it wounded. The curate wept the more, and yet the weeping seemed to loosen something that had been locked tight inside him.

Brown rose and helped the curate to his feet, and said again, with quiet firmness, that he would tell nobody what he knew, and that no one would ever hear it from him. The next step, he said, must be Wilfred's own choice, for no man can be made honest by force, and he would not take from him the dignity of choosing. Then he turned and waited, with his hands resting on his umbrella and his eyes fixed kindly on the wall.

They went down the winding stair in silence, round and round in the dark, with the light fading slowly above them and the old stone cold under their hands. At the bottom the church door stood open, and the sunlight of the village poured in as if the world had been washed. Wilfred stopped on the threshold with his eyes closed, as a man stops who is about to dive into deep water.

Then he opened his eyes and walked slowly down the steep street toward the smithy yard, with his head up and his step firm, and Brown followed a little way behind. The villagers stepped aside as he passed, and no one spoke, for there was something in the curate's face that silenced them. He had grown suddenly older, and yet in some strange way he looked at peace.

At the gate of the smithy yard Wilfred stopped in front of the inspector and said, in a voice that was low but perfectly clear, that he had something to tell him. Then, without any flourish and without any excuse, he said that it was he who had killed his brother. Nobody moved, and for a moment even the wind seemed to hold its breath.

The inspector stared at him in amazement, and a gasp ran through the crowd like wind through a field of grass. The doctor, who had been thinking about the two hints, remembered the long drop from the church tower and the flying hammer, and at last he understood how a small tool could kill a strong man. He turned to look for Father Brown, but the little priest had slipped away behind the crowd.

The blacksmith was set free at once, and his red-haired wife ran across the yard and threw her arms round him, weeping now for joy rather than sorrow. The villagers, who a few minutes earlier had been ready to hang him, stood quiet and a little ashamed, and no one would meet his eye. He put his huge hand gently on his wife's head and said a short prayer in a low voice.

Father Brown walked quietly away up the steep street, with his umbrella under his arm and his round face turned toward the sky, and nobody thanked him, for nobody knew all that he had done. Above him the church tower stood over the village in the clear light, tall and grey and silent, as it had stood for centuries. It was only a small hammer, he reflected, but it had been dropped from a very great height.

The Sign of the Broken Sword opens on a night of such hard frost that the ground rang under the feet and the stars seemed to be made of ice. Father Brown and his friend Flambeau stood in a dark churchyard before the great metal tomb of General Sir Arthur St Clare, which gleamed faintly in the moonlight like a thing of silver. It was a monument that thousands of English people came to visit as if it were a shrine.

General St Clare had been one of the great heroes of his country, a soldier of famous courage and of spotless honour, and his tomb had become a place of pilgrimage. Visitors came from all over England to lay wreaths and flowers before it, and some of them stood there for a long time in silence, with their hats in their hands. Even in the frozen moonlight the metal gave off a solemn glow, as if it were still keeping watch over the nation.

Brown turned from the tomb and asked his friend, in an abstracted way, where a wise man would hide a leaf. Flambeau, who was used to the priest's riddles, answered with a shrug that it was easy enough, for the wise man would hide it in the forest. Brown nodded slowly, as though the answer were exactly what he had expected, and seemed neither pleased nor displeased by it.

Then Brown asked what the wise man would do if there happened to be no forest, and Flambeau, who could not see the point of the question, shook his head. Brown said in a low, unhappy voice that the wise man would grow a forest to hide the leaf in, and the words hung in the cold air like smoke. He did not explain them, and Flambeau, who knew his friend's habits, did not ask him to do so.

The two friends left the churchyard and set out along a frozen road that ran through a great dark forest, where the trees stood black and still against the starlit sky. Their boots rang on the hard ground, and their breath rose in clouds, and from somewhere far off came the cry of an owl. They were bound for a small inn on the other side of the wood, where they had agreed to spend the night.

As they walked, Brown said that he would tell the story of General St Clare, which every Englishman knows from his boyhood, and he asked Flambeau to listen to it as though he had never heard it. There was a note in his voice that Flambeau had learned to respect, the note of a man who is about to open a locked door. They walked on together along the glittering road, and the silent forest seemed to listen with them.

Brown began with the war in Brazil, where General St Clare had fought against the Brazilian leader Olivier, a man famous for his nobility and his chivalry to his enemies. At a place called Black River the general had attacked Olivier's army with a force that was pitifully small, and the attack had seemed to everyone an act of sheer, reckless daring. It was a battle that every schoolboy learned, and no schoolboy ever asked why it was fought.

The little English force was beaten and swallowed up, and General St Clare was taken prisoner, and some time later he was found hanged from a tree with his own broken sword hung round his neck. The whole of England had wept for him, and the sight of the broken blade had become the nation's picture of treachery and cruelty. Flambeau, who knew the story as well as anyone in England, nodded in the darkness and waited for him to go on.

Flambeau answered impatiently that he knew the tale well enough, and that it was a sad one but hardly a mystery. A brave general had attacked too boldly, had been beaten by a stronger enemy, and had been hanged in the savage way of such wars, and there was an end of it. He could not imagine what the priest could possibly find to add to a story that every child had been taught.

Brown said that there were two questions which nobody ever thought to ask about the story, and that the whole truth lay between them. Why had a clever general attacked with so small a force, he wondered, and why had a noble and chivalrous enemy hanged a helpless prisoner with a broken sword about his neck? Flambeau stopped in the road and stared at him, for he had never thought of either question.

Brown took a small book from his pocket, a life of the general written by Captain Keith, who was to marry St Clare's daughter, and held it up to the white light of the moon. The captain wrote as a loyal friend and a fond admirer, and his pages were full of praise, and yet for that reason they were the more useful. Brown turned the leaves with his gloved fingers until he found the passage he wanted.

The first clue, Brown said, was a single line in the captain's book, which declared that St Clare was no fool and that Olivier was no brute. Both statements were doubtless true, he went on, and yet a clever man had flung himself at an army with a handful of soldiers, and a gentleman had hanged a captured foe with a broken sword for a collar. Something was wrong, and the captain, in his loyal blindness, had written down the very proof.

The second clue was in the report that Olivier himself had written to his government, and Brown quoted it from memory. In plain and generous words the Brazilian praised the English for the courage of their last stand, and he wrote of the fallen with the respect that one soldier owes another. It was not the language, Brown observed, of a man who hanged his prisoners.

Flambeau strode ahead through the dark trees, guessing aloud as he went, and the more he guessed the more confident he became. Perhaps the general, he suggested, had feared the madness of his family and flung his men at the enemy to find a soldier's death, and when that too was denied him he had taken his own life.
