It was a clean and reasonable theory, and it explained the small force very well.

Brown shook his head sadly and said that it was a clean story, a story fit for a monument, but that the truth was a great deal worse. A man who has killed himself does not hang himself with a broken sword round his neck, he added, for the broken sword was a sign made by other hands. Flambeau fell silent, and the two men walked on side by side under the frozen branches, with the truth hanging between them.

Brown spoke next of Colonel Clancy, an Irish officer who had served under St Clare in that terrible war and had lived to be an old man. In his last illness, as the priest had been told by those who sat with him, Clancy had cried out against a sword and cursed it over and over until he could say no more. It was a small thing, Brown said, to put beside the great monument, but it had stayed in his mind.

Then Brown spoke of Major Murray, a stern and silent officer from Ulster, who was known for his hardness and his honesty and who had no patience for flatterers. He had died in the war, like so many others, and his body had been carried home and buried in Belfast with the honours of a soldier. Nobody in all that great and famous story seemed ever to have found it strange that a single soldier should be sent home alone.

The third man in the story, said Brown, was Espado, a Brazilian spy whom his enemies called the Vulture. After the war Espado's private papers had fallen into English hands, and among them, strangely, there had been a soldier's diary written in the English language. Brown had read it once, long ago, and he had not forgotten a single word of what it said.

The diary told how the general, riding a white horse, had drawn Major Murray aside one night and talked with him in a low voice, and how soon afterwards he had given the order to attack. The writer of the diary had seen the general come back alone, and he had noticed, with a soldier's eye, that there was something odd about the general's sword. Nobody, the writer noted with a shiver, had ever seen Major Murray alive again after that night.

Brown paused on the frozen road and asked Flambeau what he made of all these clues, the curse, the book, the dispatch and the diary. Flambeau frowned at the stars and admitted that he could see nothing but a handful of scattered facts, like beads without a string. Brown said, very quietly, that the string was a broken sword, and that it was lying in a place where nobody had thought to look.

Brown stopped in the middle of the road and said, with his usual mildness, that the other half of the broken sword lay in the grave of Major Murray, in the churchyard at Belfast. Flambeau stared at him as if the priest had spoken in a foreign language, for it was the last thing in the world that he had expected. He opened his mouth to speak, but for once in his noisy and adventurous life no words came.

Brown went on to explain that the general's sword had snapped when he used it, and that the broken tip had remained in the body of the man he had struck. The tip had gone into the earth with the body at Belfast, and no one had looked for it, because no one knew that it was there. The blade that hung round St Clare's neck was the rest of the same sword, and it was the only evidence that anybody ever saw.

Then Brown returned to his riddle and said that he had now answered it. A wise man hides a leaf in the forest, he repeated, but where there is no forest, he grows one, and a man who needs to hide a dead body must make a field of dead bodies to hide it. Flambeau understood at last that the priest was speaking of an entire battle, and he felt a cold shiver run down his back.

To hide the death of one man, said Brown, the general had led his own army into a battle that could not be won. At Black River the field was soon covered with the dead, English and Brazilian together, and among all those fallen soldiers one body more or less could never be noticed. It was the most terrible forest that a man had ever grown, and it had been planted for a single leaf.

Brown said that the noble St Clare, the hero whose tomb they had just left, had in truth been a traitor, and that for money he had sold the secrets of his army to the spy Espado. It was the one fault that the English had not been able to forgive, and the one that a proud man would kill to hide. Flambeau heard him in a silence that was almost pain, for he had grown up on the legend of St Clare like everyone else.

Major Murray, who was stern and honest and who watched everything, found out about the treachery, and on the fatal night he faced the general with what he knew. St Clare, trapped and desperate, killed him with his own sword, and the blade snapped in the wound, leaving the tip behind. That was the strangeness that the soldier in the diary had seen in the general's sword.

At dawn the general gave the order to attack with his small force, knowing very well that it must fail, and the soldiers marched out in good order, because they believed that he was the bravest of men. They were brave themselves, and they died in great numbers on that hot hill, and one body among them, which had been laid carefully among the fallen, was never noticed by anyone. The plan had been cruel beyond words, but it had been perfect, and for many years nobody had suspected it.

On that hot hill the English soldiers fought bravely until most of them had fallen, and the few who survived turned their faces at last toward their white-haired general. Slowly, one by one, they began to understand that the battle had had no purpose but to hide a crime, and that their comrades had died for a lie. Among those who understood was Colonel Clancy, the Irishman, and Clancy was a man who could not forgive.

In their anger and their shame the surviving officers hanged the general from a tree, and they hung his broken sword round his neck as the only judgement that they dared to pass. Then they agreed together, in silence, to tell the world that the enemy had done it, so that the good name of the army should be saved. It was an act of vengeance, and it was also an act of love for the country that they had served.

The surviving officers swore a solemn oath never to tell the truth, because the honour of the army and the happiness of the general's daughter seemed to them more important than justice. Years afterward, when Colonel Clancy lay dying, the memory of that night rose up in him, and it was then that he cursed the sword with his last breath. The secret had been kept for a generation, and it had been kept well.

Flambeau walked on for a long time without speaking, his great shoulders bowed, and the sound of his footsteps was the only answer that he gave. The hero of England, the soldier of spotless honour, had been a thief and a murderer, and the whole nation had knelt before his tomb for years. It was a thought hard enough for any man, and he turned it over and over like a coin in the dark.

At last Flambeau asked whether anyone could ever prove what Brown had told him, and the priest answered that nobody could, since the only proof was a piece of broken steel lying in a grave in Belfast. He had put the story together, he added, from a curse, a book, a dispatch and a diary, and he would not have it believed as certain by anyone who had not seen all four. He spoke humbly, as always, and without the least pride in having read so great a mystery from so few signs.

Flambeau asked what they should do with the secret now that they held it, and Brown answered that the general's daughter was soon to marry Captain Keith, and that the truth, if it were told, would break her heart. The dead could not be hurt by it, he said, for they had paid for everything in full, but the living could be hurt very badly. He seemed to be thinking of one particular face, young and trusting, that would be changed for ever by the news.

Brown said that if they kept the secret, no innocent person would be blamed and no guilty person escape, for the general had paid for his crime long ago and in the most terrible way. The men who had hanged him had been punished only by their own memories, and perhaps it was enough. He bent and looked at a frozen puddle that shone under the moon, and said no more for a time.

Flambeau nodded slowly and said that he agreed, and that he would take the secret to his own grave rather than see an innocent girl made unhappy. The two friends walked on together until the trees began to thin, and between the last black trunks they could see a pale stretch of open country, silver with frost. The long wood had been a kind of church to them, and they left it in a quiet mood.

Far ahead of them a warm yellow light shone against the frost, small and steady, like a star that had come down to earth. It was the window of the inn where they meant to spend the night, and after the cold of the churchyard and the long dark road it looked like the most welcoming sight in England. Flambeau quickened his pace, and even the little priest, who was never in a hurry, seemed glad to see it.

They came to the door of the inn and looked up, and above it, swinging a little in the frosty air, hung a painted wooden sign with a sword broken in two. It was the Sign of the Broken Sword, and it was a strange chance that the inn should bear such a name on such a night. Flambeau burst into a short laugh, and Brown only smiled, as a man smiles who has heard a joke he understands too well.

They went in out of the frost, and the warmth of the room struck them like a hand. A fire burned in a wide hearth, a few villagers sat talking at a long table, and the landlord, who seemed to know nothing of broken swords, welcomed the two black-coated strangers with a smile. The friends took the seats nearest the fire and called for something hot to drink.

Flambeau, warming his great hands before the fire, asked the little priest how he had come to understand crime so well, when he himself had never committed one. Brown answered mildly that he had listened to so many confessions that he knew how evil thinks, and that it was as plain to him as the road at his own door. He added, with a small smile, that it taught him how very little a man needs to be a villain, and how much to be a saint.

They sat side by side before the fire, the huge former thief and the small, shabby priest, while the frost whitened the windows and the wind swung the painted sword outside the door. The secret of the great monument was safe with the two of them, and perhaps the old general had at last found something like peace. Somewhere beyond the dark forest another crime was waiting to be understood, but for tonight Father Brown asked for nothing more than a warm drink and a seat by the fire.
